CHARLES DARWIN

The thousands of specimens Darwin collected are kept, along with millions of others, at the Darwin Centre in London’s Natural History Museum.

Temperature and humidity are precisely controlled to preserve dead animals that are often several hundred years old. A giant, eight-story cocoon- shaped building houses the entomology and botanical specimens: the so-called “dry” collections.

Specimens in alcohol—the “spirit” collections—are kept in a separate building.

PRESERVING SCIENCE

3&"$)*/('03&953&.&4tEXPLORING FOR SCIENCE As a young man, Darwin was influenced by the ideas of British philosopher William Paley, who held that the complexity found in nature was evidence that it had been designed by a god. Most naturalists of the time also believed that species were fixed. By 1837, when he first drew an evolutionary tree (below), Darwin had formulated his new theory that species developed through gradual change under selection pressure from the environment, and that complexity could evolve by this process. He was reluctant to publish the theory before he had fully developed it, but was urged to do so in 1856, when Alfred Russel Wallace published a paper outlining similar ideas.

In his book, Darwin set out what he described as “one long argument.” Many of his scientific peers immediately recognized its importance, and friends ensured that he was granted a full state funeral when he died in 1882.

As Fitzroy reported, “had not Mr.

Darwin, and two or three of the men, run to them instantly they would have been swept away irrecoverably.” The Beagle returned to Montevideo and Darwin now set off on his longest inland tour. The ship carried him down to the Negro River, Brazil, from where he rode across the Colorado River to Bahia, a distance of some 200 miles (300 km) through semi-desert. In a letter to his cousin, Darwin wrote: “My object in all this galloping was to understand the Geology of those beds which so remarkably abound with the bones of large & extinct quadrupeds.

I have partly succeeded in this; but the country is difficult to make out—every thing in America is on such a grand scale, the same formations extend for 5 or 600 miles without the slightest change.” During his journey, Darwin collected plant, animal, and fossil specimens. His notes show his theorizing: “I had been deeply impressed by discovering in the Pampean formation great fossil animals covered with armor like that on the existing armadillos; secondly by the manner in which closely allied animals replace one another in proceeding southwards over the Continent.” By April 1835, the Beagle had made a visit to the Falkland Islands, before rounding Cape Horn and commencing survey work on the west coast of South America. In February of that year, while at Valdivia, Chile, Darwin experienced the aftershocks of a major earthquake and witnessed the destruction in the town of Concepción, “It is the most awful spectacle I ever beheld. The town of Concepción is now nothing more than piles & lines of bricks, tiles & timbers … the ground is traversed by rents, the solid rocks are shivered, solid buttresses 6–10 feet thick are broken into fragments like so much biscuit.” Darwin undertook two more expeditions into the Andes, where he described the landscape as “on so grand a scale, and the atmosphere so clear & brilliant, that the whole was to me like entering on a new Planet.” High in the mountains, he found seashells and fossil tress that had grown on a sandy beach, clues that the mountains had risen after life had begun. rejoined the Beagle, which had been refitting at the Port of Coquimbo and sailed up the coast to the port of Callao near Lima, Peru. Darwin had already collected a large number of samples by this point, but he was about to embark on the most significant visit of the whole voyage.

THE GALÁPAGOS ARCHIPELAGO On September 7, 1835, the ship sailed from Callao, headed for the Galápagos Archipelago. It was here that Darwin added to his observations that species were not fixed but evolved according to their environment. He observed what became known as “Darwin’s Finches”: the 15 different species of bird, each adapted to the conditions of individual islands. During the five weeks that the Beagle sailed between the islands, Darwin recorded that “the natural history of this archipelago is very remarkable: it seems to be a little world within itself; the greater number of its inhabitants, both vegetable and animal, being found nowhere else.” After the Galápagos, the purpose of the voyage changed from coastal surveying to determining longitudes as the ship completed a circumnavigation of the Earth, sailing via Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia to Mauritius and the Cape of Good Hope.

After returning to Plymouth in October 1836, Charles Darwin embarked on what was to become his life’s work: cataloging his specimens, first in London and then at his family home in Kent. He published his detailed travel notes in 1839 as The Voyage of the Beagle before turning to the assessment of his collections, which ranged from birds and beetles to seeds, sharing his ideas with others and requesting samples from colleagues around the world. In 1856, he began to prepare a major book but Alfred Russel Wallace’s (see pp. 272–75)

paper on natural selection in 1858 forced him to produce an abstract of this major work. This was published in 1859 as On the Origin of the Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life.

HIRAM BINGHAM

SCIENTIFIC EXPLORER OF INCA RUINS

UNITED STATES

1875–1956 As a young historian, Hiram Bingham was inspired to explore South America by reading the accounts of German explorer Alexander von Humboldt. His dream was to find the fabled lost city of Vilcabamba, where the last Incas had held out against Spanish rule. Bingham mistakenly thought he had found Vilcabamba when he was led along mountainous jungle trails to a ruined city high in the Peruvian Andes. This was Machu Picchu, which proved to be one of the most sensational archeological finds of the 20th century.

organize the Yale Peruvian Expedition, which was sponsored by National Geographic magazine.

TALES OF A LOST CITY

The team set out in 1911 along the Urubamba Valley, where they uncovered a major Inca site at Llactapata. Just over a week into their trek, the party arrived at the town of Aguas Calientes. There, Bingham was told by a local farmer, Melchor Arteaga, that just a few miles away were the ruins of the city of Machu Picchu (“Old Mountain” in Quechua). Arteaga promised to guide Bingham to the site.

Others of the party were not interested in joining Bingham, so the next morning, in drizzling rain, he set off with Arteaga, accompanied only by a translator, one Sergeant Carrasco, and a small boy who would guide him through the ruined city. The three Peruvians led the way across the Urubamba River on a rickety log bridge before they came upon jungle clearances that were being farmed. Bingham noted: “A flight of beautifully constructed terraces, each two hundred yards [200 m] long and ten feet [3 m] high, had recently been rescued from the jungle.” They proceeded across the terraces before they came upon “a maze of beautiful granite houses! They were covered with trees and moss and the growth of centuries.” Born the son of missionaries on Hawaii, Bingham completed his post-graduate studies at Harvard in 1905 to become an academic specializing in Latin American history.

His first expedition in 1906 saw him retracing the journeys through Colombia and Venezuela of Simón Bolívar, the 19th-century hero of South America’s wars of independence.

Inspired by the experience, he returned to South America in 1909 and traveled by mule from Buenos Aires in Argentina across the continent to Peru. Upon seeing the spectacular ruins of the ancient Inca capital city of Cuzco, Bingham resolved to discover as much as he could about historic Inca sites. He returned home to

INCA BEER

With the permission of the Peruvian government, Bingham excavated more than 45,000 artifacts from Machu Picchu, including ornate beer storage vessels such as this.

ANCESTRAL HOME OF THE INCAS

At first, Bingham believed he had come upon the site of Tampu-tocco, the ancestral city home of the Inca people. He recorded in his journal that it “might prove to be the largest and most important ruin discovered in South America since the Spaniards arrived.” Bingham returned to the site in 1912 to remove the dense overgrowth from those structures that had not been cleared by the local people. His party included George Eaton, a bones expert, and Herbert Gregory, a geologist. During their excavation, Bingham and Eaton took more than 11,000 photographs of the site. Bingham made his third and final visit in 1915 to map the ancient Inca roads that had originally led to the city.

As time passed, Bingham became convinced that he had discovered not only the origins of Inca civilization but also the site of Vilcabamba, explaining his theory in his 1948 best-seller, Lost City of the Incas. In 1964, American Gene Savoy established the true ruins of Vilcabamba at nearby Espíritu Pampa, a site that Bingham had visited and rejected as of minor importance.

EXCAVATION TEAM

On Bingham’s second visit to Machu Picchu in 1912, he organized an extensive excavation of the site to uncover the areas that had been left untouched by the local farmers. Some of his Peruvian workers are pictured here working on an area labeled Burial Cave Number 11.

THOR HEYERDAHL

EXPLORER OF THE OCEANS BY REED RAFT

NORWAY

1914–2002 Maverick anthropologist Thor Heyerdahl completed several remarkable voyages on craft made from reed and papyrus. His goal was to find evidence that ancient mariners could have crossed the world’s oceans. Some of Heyerdahl’s theories about trans-oceanic contacts have not stood the test of time, but his voyages showed how it was indeed possible to sail the world using only simple technology. He also earned respect for his campaigns for environmental issues and world peace.

of metal implements, using only the simple tools that would have existed in pre-Columbian Peru.

SETTING SAIL

The voyage began on April 28, 1947, in the fast-moving Humboldt Current off Callao, on the coast of Peru. With each swell, the nine logs that formed the main structure would each move independently, so that sleeping on rush mats was like “lying on the back of a large, breathing animal.” Concerns over friction-wear to the ropes that held the entire structure together were dismissed within the first two weeks of the voyage, since the rope, swollen with water, embedded itself into the softened wood, strengthening rather than weakening the structure.

In 1937, Heyerdahl abandoned his studies at the University of Oslo to pursue his interest in the cultures of the Pacific. He spent time on the island of Fatu-Hiva in the Marquesas group, where he became convinced that people had migrated to Polynesia from South America, not from Southeast Asia, as was believed at the time.

Ten years later, Heyerdahl set out to prove this theory by retracing the route of the supposed prehistoric migrants. Along with four fellow Norwegians and a Swede, he began the construction of a raft, which he named the Kon-Tiki, in honor of a pre-Incan Sun god.

The raft was made from balsa-wood, reed, and rush matting, with a square sail and a steering paddle at the stern. IN HIS FOOTSTEPS

“THE FIRST HIPPY” Heyerdahl ﬁrst developed his theories during an 18-month stay on Fatu-Hiva in 1937–38. His diaries from there (below)

formed the basis of his book Back to Nature (1974).

On July 30, after 90 days at sea, the men made their first sighting of land. Land fall was finally made at the island of Angatau, where Heyerdahl was jubilant: “I shall never forget that wade across the reef … I slipped off my shoes and thrust my bare toes into the warm, bone-dry sand.” The Kon-Tiki voyage had taken 101 days across 4,000 miles (6,500 km) of the Pacific Ocean, and Heyerdahl had proved that his craft could achieve the journey. His film of the voyage received an Oscar in 1951 for best documentary, while his book of the expedition sold millions of copies worldwide.

DISPUTED THEORIES

In 1955–56, Heyerdahl led an archeological expedition to Rapanui, or Easter Island, seeking to prove that its people had arrived from South America. In 1969, he built a boat from papyrus called Ra, after the Egyptian Sun god, to prove that ancient mariners could have crossed the Atlantic from Africa. His first attempt was a failure, but he succeeded a year later in Ra II. In 1978, he sailed through the Persian Gulf against the wind on another reed boat, the Tigris.

Heyerdahl’s many theories were always widely disputed, and recent DNA evidence shows that he was sometimes wrong, but his commitment to his cause earned respect from his critics. His intrepid voyages are testimony to the power of human endeavor and ingenuity.

EASTER ISLAND

Heyerdahl theorized that the statues of Easter Island bore a striking resemblance to the art of Peru, and that they had been built by people of South American origin.

ABOARD THE KON–TIKI After initial alarm as its balsa-wood frame became dangerously sodden, the Kon-Tiki proved itself seaworthy and lasted the 101-day journey across the Paciﬁc Ocean.

THOR HEYERDAHL

In about 1000ce, Viking voyagers sought opportunities for migration and settlement in the Arctic. By the 16th century, however, the motivation of Arctic explorers had changed.

The Spanish and Portuguese controlled sea routes from Europe to East Asia via the Indian Ocean, and a race began among northern European nations to establish new routes by way of a Northwest or Northeast Passage.

A PASSAGE TO THE PACIFIC

Early attempts to cross the Arctic Ocean were unsuccessful. Willem Barentsz’s attempts to find a Northeast Polar Passage from Europe to the Pacific from 1594–96 ended in his death (see pp. 288–89). Henry Hudson retraced Barentsz’s route in 1607, but he too was defeated by the ice (see pp. 286–87). Hudson would himself perish on a later voyage in search of a Northwest Passage. By the early 19th century, British naval expeditions had shown that it was impossible to sail over the top of the world via the Arctic Ocean, but the search for a Northwest Passage continued. When John Franklin’s expedition disappeared in 1845 (see pp. 292–93), the search parties that followed made the first detailed charts of the Canadian Arctic. They laid the groundwork for Roald Amundsen (see pp. 302–05)

finally to navigate across the top of North America in 1903–06. Three years after Amundsen’s voyage, Robert Peary claimed to have reached the North Pole on foot (see pp. 308–09). His claim was dubious, but in 1969, British explorer Wally Herbert definitely achieved this feat (see p. 309).

PUSHING SOUTH

Antarctica was the last of the continents to be explored and the first to be truly “discovered” by modern explorers. “I make bold to declare that the world will derive no benefit from it,” wrote James Cook after circumnavigating the pack-ice off the coast of the continent in 1772 (see pp. 156–59). Cook had been the first to cross the Antarctic Circle, but he did not reach Antarctica itself. Thirty years earlier, a young French navigator, Jean- Baptiste Charles Bouvet de Lozier, had made the same assessment of the commercial potential of the supposed Terra Australis (“Southern Land”). De Lozier encountered icebergs, which he described as “floating rocks,” and temperatures so extreme that the sailors literally cried with cold in their inadequate clothing. Failing in his goal to find new lands for France, de Lozier recorded that “it was not the men who had failed the mission, but the mission that had failed the men.” Britain, Russia, and the United States all aimed to be the first to reach the land thought to lie to the south of the ice mass in the Antarctic.

In 1820, there were three competing claims of being the first to sight Antarctica: from the British naval officer Edward Bransfield, the American sealer Nathaniel Palmer, and the Russian explorer Fabian von Bellingshausen.

The years that followed saw an explosion in the sealing trade with hundreds of American and British ships operating in the seas off the Antarctic Peninsula.

HEAT-CONSERVING FOOTWEAR

Amundsen imitated the fur-lined animal skin clothing the Inuit wore after observing the protection it offered in the polar extremes.

In 1822–24, British sailor James Weddell reached the then farthest point south, achieving a position at 74°15’S at 34°16’45’’W.

Weddell was the first to measure wind and seismic activity in Antarctica. He also systematically recorded the wildlife, including a detailed biology of the king penguin.

SCIENTIFIC EXPLORERS

Commercial interests aside, the British Royal Navy led the way in the 1840s, despatching James Clark Ross in command of the Erebus and Terror on the Antarctic Circumpolar Voyage. In the period 1839–43, Ross would lead a scientific expedition, in the company of the botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker, which would provide three seasons’ worth of charting, geographical, and meteorological observation, and the collection of 1,500 plant specimens stored in a specially constructed herbarium on board the Terror.

The expedition discovered the Ross Sea, the Ross Ice Shelf, Ross Island, and Victoria Land, and identified the volcano Mount Erebus (which Ross named after his ship). Ross had laid the

TRAIL BLAZER

In 1899, Norwegian Carsten Borchgrevink became the ﬁrst explorer to reach the Ross Ice Shelf since James Clark Ross 60 years earlier.

He paved the way for Amundsen and Scott.

THE RACE FOR LAND RIGHTS

Australian Douglas Mawson raised the British ﬂag on King George Land in 1931. Later expeditions such as his were motivated largely by the desire to establish sovereignty on the continent.

foundation for future British exploration of the continent. In 1895, the Sixth International Geographical Congress in London declared exploration of the Antarctic to be “the greatest piece of geographical exploration still to be undertaken.” Belgian Adrien de Gerlache led the first Antarctic expedition of this new “Heroic Age” in 1897–99, and just over a decade later, Roald Amundsen famously beat Robert Scott (see pp. 312–15) in this tragic race to the Pole. By the time of Shackleton’s death in 1922 (see pp. 318–19), the coast of the Antarctic continent had been surveyed, its highest mountain climbed, and the South Pole reached.

“TOY OF THE ELEMENTS” Erich von Drygalski led the ﬁrst German Antarctic Expedition in 1901–03. He reached as far south as 66°2’ before his ship, the Gauss (shown here), became trapped in the pack-ice.

Drygalski described having “become a toy of the elements” as his ship froze.

Mariner and trailblazing explorer Henry Hudson made a series of expeditions in search of an Arctic trade route from Europe to China. His travels also took him on the first significant exploration of two of the largest geographical features of the North American continent—the river and bay that now bear his name. Although a skilled seafarer, Hudson was prone to lapses of judgment and repeatedly failed to exert authority over his crew, a weakness that would ultimately prove his undoing.

His name first appears in the records of a 1607 expedition funded by the Muscovy Company of London, which was searching for the elusive Far East trade route thought to pass through the Arctic.

INTO THE ARCTIC

Hudson set out on May 1, 1607, aboard the Hopewell, a small vessel that held a crew of 10, sailing northwest across the Atlantic Ocean.

He reached Greenland 43 days later then turned northeast, reaching as far as the archipelago of Svalbard (Spitsbergen). Progress was hampered by “mountains” of coastal ice and “thicke fog, cold and slabbie weather.” Hudson returned to England having sailed 750 miles (1,200 km) past the Arctic Circle—farther north than any other explorer had yet traveled.

In April 1608, he attempted a second journey to the Far East, this time reaching the islands of Novaya Zemlya (now Russia) before the ice became too thick for the Hopewell. It was there that the first sign of a worrying character flaw became apparent: Hudson wanted to turn west to continue the search, but relented under protest from his crew, who were eager to go home.

When Hudson returned without success, the Muscovy Company withdrew its support. He 3&"$)*/('03&953&.&4t505)&&/%40'5)&&"35)

EXPLORING THE HUDSON

The Half Moon reached the point at which the Hudson River narrows, now the site of the city of Albany. The event is commemorated on this medal.

MAPS WITH GAPS

This 1608 map by Dutchman Jadocus Hondius the Senior reveals how little was known of the Arctic and American interior in Hudson’s time. It was even thought that the North Pole was ice-free in summer due to the Sun’s heat, clearing a passage to the Far East.

HENRY HUDSON

next turned to the Dutch East India Company and terms were soon agreed to, including strict instructions to take a route east. Hudson left Amsterdam on the Half Moon in March 1609 with a Dutch and English crew, but when the men encountered pack-ice they pressed him to head west instead, toward the warmer New World. Rather than quelling the rebellion—and despite the terms of his contract—Hudson gave in, and reached North America in July 1609.

TROUBLE IN THE RANKS

In September, Hudson wrote “we came to three great rivers … rode in five fathoms and saw many salmon, mullets, and rays very great.” The Half Moon stood at the mouth of a vast river that Hudson believed might hold the fabled passage to the Far East, so he set out to chart its course, naming it the Hudson River. But, despite plentiful fishing and friendly locals, the crew threatened mutiny. After reaching present-day Albany, some 140 miles (225 km) upriver, Hudson set sail for home.

On his return to London, Hudson escaped the ire of his Dutch employers only to be arrested for flying the flag of the Netherlands. But he still won support for a repeat English expedition and set sail on the Discovery in April 1610. Hudson again showed his lack of mettle by not challenging the inclusion of Colebrune, a man sent by his employers to keep an eye on him.

Instead, Hudson deviously left port without him. Two months later, Hudson passed through a treacherous strait to reach the wide, open expanse that was later named Hudson Bay. Failing to find a passage to Southeast Asia, he took the boat south into the bay where it soon froze into the ice. Forced to overwinter and with limited supplies, the men endured scurvy, hostile natives, and the cold. In June 1611, as soon as the ice had melted sufficiently to return home, the crew mutinied, casting Hudson and his young son, along with six others, adrift.

Nothing was heard of them again. Eight of the 13 mutineers survived the journey home. All were arrested, but none was convicted of any crime. This may have been from lack of evidence, or because they had returned with valuable information about the New World.

Barentsz’s first expedition was funded by the merchants of Amsterdam. His orders were to discover a northeast route to the kingdoms of China. On June 5, 1594, four ships set out from Texel in Holland, and sailed north of Norway toward Muscovia (present-day Russia). They found the wreck of a ship as they approached the islands of Novaya Zemlya, proof that the area had previously been visited.

DEFEATED BY THE PACK-ICE

On the night of July 13, the ships sailed into what Barentsz described as a “plaine [sic] field of ice,” which they edged around before spying Novaya Zemlya to the southeast, where they found great numbers of seals and walruses.

On his third voyage, Barentsz ﬁrst sailed northwest to Spitsbergen (shown here), which he mistook for the eastern shores of Greenland, before turning back to the east.

WILLEM BARENTSZ

SEARCHER FOR A NORTHEAST PASSAGE

NETHERLANDS

c. 1550–97 As an experienced cartographer and navigator, Willem Barentsz was well qualified to lead the Dutch merchants’ search for new trading routes to the East in the 16th century.

He did so by sailing north through the icy wastes of the “White Sea,” as he described the Arctic Ocean. Barentsz’s three voyages, although unsuccessful, would do much to chart the coastline of Siberia, while his final voyage demonstrated to Europeans that it was possible to survive a winter locked in the Arctic ice.

IN HIS FOOTSTEPS

Recognizing the agility of both creatures once in the water, Barentsz commanded his men to kill them and seize their prized teeth on land, but they broke “all their hatchets and pikes in pieces and could not kill one of them.” Barentsz took his ship around an island he named the Island of Orange, but the ice hampered progress, so he headed south to rejoin the other ships. There, one of his captains, Brandt Ysbrandtszoon, described seeing an open sea, beyond which he was convinced lay a clear way to the Kingdom of Cathay (China).

WILLEM BARENTSZ

HUMILIATING FAILURE

A second voyage was organized, and this time seven ships were despatched, five of them loaded with goods to be traded. On August 21, 1595, the fleet reached the place described by Ysbrandtszoon and made a landing. Barentsz’s men saw well-worn pathways but found no one.

Two ships were commissioned, captained by Jacob van Heemskerch and Jan Corneliszoon Rijp. Barentsz this time acted as pilot to Heemskerch. On June 9, 1596, they came to a new island, which they named Bear Island, before continuing north as the ice floes steadily increased, sighting Spitsbergen on June 19.

They set their course northwest, but the polar ice stopped them in their tracks. After returning to Bear Island, the two ships took separate routes, with Barentsz sailing east toward Novaya Zemlya.

A WINTER ON THE ICE

On August 7, 1596, Barentsz’s ship was frozen into the ice. The historian Gerrit de Veer described how they were “forced, in great cold, poverty, misery and greife [sic] to stay all winter.” The men endured the winter without enough food. On May 11 the following year, the ship was finally able to depart. Barentsz himself had been ill for several weeks and died during the return journey.

WILLEM BARENTSZ

THE ICE ABOUT THE LAND

LED AND HINDERED US

FILLING IN THE ARCTIC MAP

This map, from Gerrit de Veer’s0CTTCVKXGQHVJG.CUV8Q[CIG QH9KNNGO$CTGPVU\, clearly marks the western coastline of Novaya Zemlya. Its eastern coast had not been charted.

They attempted to sail farther east, but were once again defeated by the ice fields and turned back for home. The voyage had been an expensive failure, but the merchants, frustrated by their lack of access to the east, pressed their case. By the following spring, Barentsz had secured a third expedition.

BEAR ATTACK

On Barentsz’s ﬁrst voyage in 1594, his men shot a polar bear that was climbing on board. On the second voyage, a polar bear attacked and killed two of Barentsz’s men.

NORDENSKIÖLD

FIRST NAVIGATOR OF THE NORTHEAST PASSAGE

FINLAND

1832–1901 A mineralogist and geologist with an insatiable scientific curiosity, Nordenskiöld is best remembered for being the first to navigate the Northeast Passage in 1878. Finding a viable shipping lane between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans along the northern coast of Russia had been an ambition of European explorers since the 16th century. This Nordenskiöld accomplished in his modern steamship, the Vega. His achievement inspired a whole new generation of Arctic explorers.

to break through the ice floes. His observations led Nordenskiöld to think about the effects of ocean currents on the drift patterns of Arctic ice, and he concluded that by late summer the northern Arctic should be free of ice. Eager to prove his theory, he set off in July 1868 on board the steamship Sofia. It was a major scientific expedition to gauge how close to the North Pole it was possible to sail.

The Sofia headed first for Bear Island, and then pushed north to Spitsbergen. After a severe storm, the ship was holed by an iceberg, but the captain, von Otter, succeeded in steering it safely into harbor. They had reached a latitude of 81°42’N, but von Otter recorded how “we could reach this latitude only by blasting ice in many places.” Nordenskiöld had made an important, if disappointing, discovery: that the ice flowed farther south than he had expected.

His next idea was even more ambitious: to become the first person to walk to the North Pole. Several people had tried and failed since British naval officer William Parry Nordenskiöld acquired his enthusiasm for geology from his father, himself an eminent geologist and explorer. After studying the subject at the University of Helsinki, he moved to Sweden in 1857 and began his career as an explorer almost immediately. In 1858, he set off on his first expedition to Spitsbergen (in the present-day Norwegian Arctic), led by the Swedish geologist Otto Torell.

ATTEMPTS AT THE POLE

FINDING THE PASSAGE

By 1878, Nordenskiöld was onto his next theory: that it was possible to navigate from Europe to Asia by way of a northeast passage. This, too, had been an ambition of explorers for centuries. After establishing a route from Norway to the mouth of the Yenisei River in Siberia, he thought it possible that the Bering Strait would be ice-free in summer. His 300-ton steamer, the Vega, was fitted with sails and loaded with provisions for a two-year expedition. The team included Danish, Italian, and Russian scientists and officers. From mid-September, the coastal passage began to fill with drift ice, making progress slow. At Koliuchin Bay, just two days from the Bering Strait, the ship was finally trapped by the ice, 7 miles (12 km) from the coast.

Scientific research continued on board until the Vega was freed 10 months later in the summer of 1879, when it sailed on to complete its journey, becoming the first ship to sail from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It returned home along a southern route around Eurasia.

The crew of the Vega was welcomed as heroes on the return to Sweden in April 1880. The jubilation was all the greater because the crew had been cut off and feared lost during EXPLORER’S ISLAND Spitsbergen has played a major role in several famous explorations. In 1599, Willem Barentsz mapped it for the ﬁrst time (see pp. 288–89). The island was also the launching point for the airship ﬂight to the Pole of Roald Amundsen (see pp. 302–05) and the Arctic expeditions of Ernest Shackleton (see pp. 318–19).

IN HIS FOOTSTEPS

1872—Attempt at the North Pole Nordenskiöld intends to walk from Spitsbergen across the ice to the North Pole, but the expedition quickly goes wrong and no serious attempt is made 1878—Across the top of Eurasia The 8GIC sets sail from Karlskrona in Sweden, reaching Koliuchin Bay in the Chukchi Sea, where Nordenskiöld and his crew spend the winter trapped in the ice 1879–80—Return to Sweden The ice thaws sufficiently to free the 8GIC, which passes through the Bering Strait and returns to Sweden via a southern route their winter trapped in the ice. Although Nordenskiöld had delayed departure (which had led to the enforced overwintering), he had shown that it was possible to navigate the Northeast Passage in two months. He wrote up an exhaustive five-volume account of the expedition, and his research advanced the understanding of climate patterns, but it was not until decades later that the route would be used for trade.

In 1882, Nordenskiöld embarked on another challenge: an expedition on foot to Greenland’s inland ice sheet. He was forced back by technical problems, but this challenge was soon taken up by another great Scandinavian explorer, Fridtjof Nansen (see pp. 296–301).

His determination to chart the Northwest Passage—the shipping route that was thought to link the Atlantic and Pacific oceans via the Canadian Arctic—was to prove his undoing. The search for Franklin and his vanished ships and crew became an obsession that gripped his loyal—if deluded—public for decades after his death.

JOHN FRANKLIN

ARCTIC CARTOGRAPHER OF NORTH AMERICA

ENGLAND

1786–1847 Born in 1786 in Lincolnshire, Franklin joined the Royal Navy at the age of 14 and served on HMS Investigator on a voyage to Australia. After cutting his teeth on an unsuccessful expedition to find an open-water route to the North Pole in 1818, Franklin was chosen to lead an overland expedition to find the Northwest Passage the following year.

The expedition started well but soon went awry when violent feuding between Canada’s two leading trading companies in Hudson Bay prevented Franklin from buying supplies from either. Despite a lack of provisions, he pressed on obstinately, a character trait that made

The shortage of food was so extreme that men were forced to eat rock lichen and boot leather, and Franklin was known thereafter as “the man who ate his shoes.” But worse was to come.

JOHN FRANKLIN

reform had made him unpopular in the colony— he was in his fifties and might have retired. But by a twist of fate, he was given one last shot at his dream, and led another expedition to the Northwest Passage in 1845.

Advances since Franklin’s last expedition had left just 300 miles (480 km) of Arctic coastline unmapped, so confidence was high that the expedition would be a success.

The vessels chosen for the trip, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror, were equipped with the latest iron plating and steam-driven screw-propellers, and the crew was mostly seasoned hands. However, clothing for Arctic weather was lacking, and the crew-count was too high. As it later turned out, the lead sealing used in the canned provisions may have leached into the food, poisoning those who ate it. At 59 years old, Franklin’s age may also have put him at a disadvantage.

After being sighted in Lancaster Sound by the whaling vessel Enterprise in July 1845, nothing more was heard of the expedition. The ships were carrying three years’ worth of provisions so the first rescue attempt was not launched until 1847, and a further 25 expeditions— encouraged by a large reward offered—were sent to look for the missing men. The fate of the party was finally uncovered by the Fox expedition in 1859, when a body and ship’s items were found at the Back River estuary. Documents recording the point at which Erebus and Terror had become trapped in the ice in 1846 were also found, along with a record of the death of Franklin from unknown causes in 1847. The survivors had abandoned the ice-bound ships in 1848 and made for the mainland, but perished of scurvy, lead poisoning, cannibalism, and starvation.

While Franklin was hailed as a man of great courage, his obstinacy in the face of risk may twice have had fatal consequences. However, the 1859 Fox expedition revealed Franklin’s last achievement—by reaching the Back River, he had stumbled upon the missing section of the Northwest Passage.

own hands and shot Teroahauté dead. The party was only saved by the timely return of Captain Back with local guides and supplies.

Despite the expedition’s macabre ending, Franklin did not give up on his search for the Northwest Passage. His second expedition, which set off from Hudson Bay in 1825, was better planned, equipped, and executed than the first. The party successfully surveyed hundreds of miles of Arctic coastline to the east and west of the Mackenzie River, with no loss of life. Lauded as a hero on his return to England in 1827, Franklin was knighted two years later.

THE “LOST” EXPEDITION Britain’s Royal Navy rejected Franklin’s next proposals for exploring the Canadian Arctic, and it seemed that his career as an explorer was over.

REACHING FOR EXTREMES • TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH Tents are inadequate for extended use in the polar regions due to the intense cold and incessant winds, which can rage at speeds of up to 200 mph (320 kph) in Antarctica. To provide adequate shelter in such extremes, huts are needed, and with no raw materials to build one on site, the One of the main health problems encountered by polar explorers during the late 19th and early 20th centuries was the disease scurvy. The condition causes gums to swell and bleed so that teeth fall out, bleeding from the scalp, and internal bleeding around the joints.

Untreated, it usually results in death. In the 19th century, scurvy was known as the scourge of the Arctic and even Scott’s huts have to be prefabricated before departure. The location of the hut is crucial: the German Antarctic Expedition of 1911 erected theirs on an iceberg only to dismantle it hastily when the berg began to drift away from the shore. The Oxford University Arctic Expedition of 1935–36 solved the problem of wind and cold by excavating 40 tons of ice to build an underground base of several large rooms connected by tunnels.

ﬁrst Antarctic expedition of`1901 suffered from it (see pp. 312–15). Scott, Wilson, and Shackleton were forced to turn back from their attempt to reach the South Pole when they showed the early signs of scurvy. At the time, they believed that their scurvy had been caused by tainted meat. Its true cause, a deﬁciency in vitamin C, was ﬁnally established in 1932 by American chemist Charles King.

MAKING SHELTER

“SCOURGE OF THE ARCTIC”

FOOD AND WATER

Keeping going in the cold takes a lot of energy, and modern polar explorers will eat 6,000 calories a day—three times the normal adult consumption. In the past, explorers were not so well fed.

Canadian Vilhjamur Stefansson claimed in the early 20th century that, like the Inuit, explorers could live in the Arctic without vegetables by eating a low- carbohydrate all-meat diet. The staple of Stefansson’s time was Pemmican, made from pounded meat and fat, and scurvy was still common. It is now thought that the Inuit got their vitamin C from sources such as the skin of the beluga whale.

The poles are among the driest places on Earth, with less precipitation than the Sahara Desert. Drinking water can only be obtained from the ice, which means that fuel has to be carried to melt it.

FROSTBITTEN FINGERS

Edward Atkinson, the physician on Robert Scott’s 1910 Antarctic expedition, suffered this severe frostbite in his right hand.

THE DEADLY COLD

POLAR

REGIONS

Explorers have long been attracted by the bleak and deadly environments of the Arctic and Antarctica, lured by the prospects of fabled waterways, scientific achievement, and lasting fame.

A century after the poles were first reached, technology, dietary understanding, and geographical knowledge have all improved to make polar exploration safer. It is still the case, however, that only the hardiest explorers dare venture into these forbidding arenas.

experiencing life in the… The coldest temperature ever recorded was -128.6°F (-89.2°C) at the Russian Antarctic base in 1983. Temperatures only rise above freezing on the Antarctic Peninsula; the interior remains extremely cold all year. The coldest Arctic temperature ever recorded was -90°F (-68°C) in Siberia, while in the brief Arctic summer, temperatures can reach 50°F (10°C).

In extreme cold, explorers face the risk of hypothermia, which can cause death through organ failure. Frostbite is also a major risk, and can occur within minutes of exposure to extreme cold. In its mildest form, it causes skin irritation and pain; in its severest form, the muscles, tendons, and blood vessels all freeze and the affected part of the body dies. Amputation of the dead ﬂesh is usually necessary.

POLAR REGIONS

POLAR TRANSPORT

Contact with the Inuit demonstrated to early explorers and fur traders the advantage of using dogs to haul light sleds. However, the British Royal Navy stubbornly persisted with the grueling practice of using men to haul large sleds. William Edward Parry experimented with caribou when attempting to reach the North Pole in 1827, but the 20-ft (6-m) long sled-boats proved too heavy for his eight animals. American Robert Peary (see pp. 308–09) and the Norwegian Roald Amundsen (see pp. 302–05) spent time with the Inuit learning how to drive dogs. In the race to the South Pole, Amundsen’s familiarity with dogs gave him an advantage over Scott, whose Siberian ponies were unable to withstand the Antarctic conditions. The ﬁrst person to take an automobile to the Antarctic was Ernest Shackleton (see pp. 318–19) in 1907. It did not function well. Scott took motorized tractors in 1909, but again they could not cope with the cold. The ﬁrst motorized crossing of the Antarctic was made in 1957–58 by Sir Vivian Fuchs using specially built tracked Sno-Cat vehicles.

PERSONAL SAFETY

In the Antarctic, ensuring personal safety involves a simple ﬁght against the elements. In the Arctic, however, explorers are faced with people and polar bears. Most expeditions dealt with bears by shooting them, while relations with the Inuit were generally peaceful. The North Pole lies more than 430 miles (700 km) from the nearest land. The Arctic Ocean is covered by sea ice, and crossing this shifting crust is very hazardous. In his book on the British Trans-Arctic Expedition of 1968–69, Wally Herbert describes a large ice ﬂoe on which he had camped cracking in half, cutting him off from his supplies.

One of the most frightening dangers in either polar region is the possibility that an explorer may be injured or become ill, and before the days of airplanes and icebreakers the chances of being rescued were slim.

The incapacitated person is also a burden on the expedition. The desperately ill Captain Lawrence Oates famously walked to his death rather than hinder the chances of his comrades during Scott’s ill-fated expedition to the South Pole in 1912 (see pp. 312–15).

UNSUPPORTED TEAM

Ranulph Fiennes (right) and Michael Stroud pulled their own sleds for their unsupported expedition to Antarctica in 1992.

GREAT GOD THIS IS AN AWFUL PLACE

ROBERT FALCON SCOTT, UPON REACHING THE SOUTH POLE

COPING WITH EXTREMES

Intense cold, ferocious winds, blinding snow storms, a broken surface with steep cliffs and gaping crevasses: the physical environment of the polar regions provides challenges at every level. Survival requires planning. Arguably the most successful polar explorer, Roald Amundsen planned carefully, training himself in the skills he would need. Already a skilled skier, Amundsen studied medicine, seamanship, and paid particular attention to Inuit and Lapp cold- weather survival techniques.

Polar clothing needs to offer protection without restricting movement. At the time of Scott, specialized clothing had been developed, but it was not yet made of breathable materials. The men would sweat when pulling the sleds and then ﬁnd themselves cold and damp when they stopped. Their wet clothes would freeze within minutes, bringing the danger of frostbite. Scott’s colleague Apsley Cherry-Garrard wrote: “Our clothing was hard as boards and stuck out from our bodies in every imaginable angle.”

FRIDTJOF NANSEN

FRIDTJOF NANSEN

FRIDTJOF

NANSEN

REVOLUTIONARY POLAR EXPLORER

NORWAY

1861–1930 Fridtjof Nansen led the way in polar exploration during the late 19th century through his adoption of Inuit methods of travel and clothing. Famous for his willingness to take “considered risks,” Nansen would influence many future polar explorers. After his distinguished career as an oceanographer, Nansen played a significant role in the field of humanitarian aid following World War I. In 1922, he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work at the League of Nations.

As a boy in rural Norway, Nansen developed a passion for the outdoors, learning to ski and skate at an early age. In 1882, while a student of zoology at Royal Frederick University in Christiania (present-day Oslo), he joined an expedition to the Arctic Ocean on board a sealing ship called the Viking. On the journey, he made scientific observations of sea currents and ice, putting his artistic skills to good use by adding detailed sketches to his notes. The ship crossed into the Arctic Circle in mid-March and Nansen experienced the drift of the boat within the ice before the Viking was finally frozen into the pack. The ship drifted south and then north, before being released from the ice in July.

During this time, Nansen observed a piece of driftwood in the Arctic water. He hypothesized that the wood could only have floated there from Siberia, and would prove his theory correct on a later voyage. He also caught his first glimpses

Our order was death or the west coast of Greenland.” In June 1888, the men were set adrift on two boats from the sealing ship Jason, 35 miles (56 km) from land, opposite the Sermilik Fjord. Maneuvering the boats through the ice in heavy rain and fog, Nansen had no option but to drift along the east coast of Greenland looking for a suitable landing place.

One night, the men had no choice but to pitch their tent on an ice floe that Nansen warned would be “crushed into dust” if it reached the open sea. Otto Sverdrup, on watch, feared that destruction was imminent as the floe drifted seaward. He opened one hook of the tent to warn the others. He hesitated, opening one more hook, just as the current turned and the floe headed back toward land. The danger had passed. On August 10, after 55 days, the boats finally made land.

GROUNDBREAKING SLEDS

The skiers began to pull their five “Nansen” sleds across the ice cap. These were mounted on skis and equipped with sails, which were used whenever possible to speed the crossing. Their equipment included three-man sleeping bags, each made from caribou skin. Water had to be thawed from ice and was in scarce supply. On one occasion, after a meal of pea soup was spilt, the men picked up chunks of the frozen soup and swallowed it down: “No drop was lost.” Nansen described how “we only saw three things: that was snow, sun, and ourselves.” On October 12, the six men reached the west coast at Godthaab. Unable to make passage on a ship until the spring, they occupied themselves shooting and learning how to sail in Inuit kayaks. They arrived back in Christiania, by way of Copenhagen, in May 1889, to be met by a crowd of more than 40,000 cheering Norwegians.

Relying on a small group of athletic men using just skis and ski-borne sleds, Nansen’s new method of polar exploration was revolutionary. He had a theory that polar ice was carried by ocean currents from east to west. He believed that, once frozen in a northerly position in the ice of the Arctic Ocean, a ship could float across the Pole.

THE JOURNEY STARTS

Within four months of embarking on the expedition, the Fram had already become frozen in pack-ice, where she was to remain for nearly three years.

SCIENTIFIC WORK

The team on the Fram discovered through soundings that the depth of the polar basin was at least 10,800 ft (3,300 m), 10 times deeper than had been previously thought.

IN HIS FOOTSTEPS

1893–1896—The Fram’s journey The Fram drifts trapped in the ice for nearly three years, but the currents do not take it to the North Pole as Nansen had hoped 1895–96—On foot to the Pole Realizing that the Fram will not drift to the North Pole, Nansen and Johansen set out for the Pole on foot, but are forced back by bad weather; they are reunited with the crew of the Fram a year later The Fram is frozen into the ice just north of Cape Cheliuskin, a lower altitude than Nansen had hoped Nansen and Johansen spend the winter on Jackson Island, living off seal and bear meat B 1896–1930 A

FRIDTJOF NANSEN

Almost immediately after setting out, Nansen recorded the difficulties of the terrain: “one falls into the water … these baths are not an unmixed pleasure now that there is no possibility of drying or changing one’s clothes, and one must wear a chain mail of ice until they thaw and dry on the body.” On reaching a new farthest point north at 86°14’N on April 8, the two men decided that conditions were too bad and they abandoned their push to the Pole.

With this plan in mind, he had a ship specially constructed, calling it the Fram (see below). The ship was equipped with a large library to occupy the men during what would prove to be a three- year voyage. Nansen described the plan as “to drift with the drift ice and keep clear of land.” Setting out from Christiania in June 1893, the Fram sailed north by way of Tromsø in northern Norway to pick up additional skilled Arctic seamen. Nansen planned to follow Nordenskiöld’s route north, but on reaching Cape Cheliuskin (the northernmost point of mainland Russia), he found the route blocked by ice and was forced to allow the ship to freeze into the pack-ice at a latitude of 78–79°N. They drifted slowly and in an uncertain direction.

ATTEMPT ON THE POLE

By the spring of 1895, Nansen realized that the ship would not drift to the Pole. He decided to take one of his “considered risks,” setting out with the skier and gymnast Hjalmar Johansen to make an assault on the Pole, equipped with 27 dogs, two sleds, and two kayaks. With no realistic prospect of ever finding the Fram again, the two men faced a grueling return journey across the ice to the nearest known land, 500 miles (800 km)

south of their starting point.

Their return was not without danger: “the ice began to sink under the weight of the other dogs and the sled and the water came flowing up,” wrote Nansen. By August, they had reached open water and, strapping the two kayaks together to form a catamaran, made their way through a series of uninhabited islands that, unknown to them, were part of the Franz Josef Land archipelago. As winter approached, they built a shelter in the ice of Jackson Island, where they lived off seal and bear meat.

Nansen and Johansen left the island in May

1896. After traveling for a month, they were

astonished to hear English voices: quite by chance, they had come upon a British expedition led by Frederick Jackson. They were welcomed to their camp and shortly afterward sailed on a British relief ship. On reaching Tromsø, they were reunited with the crew of the Fram. The wealth of scientific data they had gathered would break new ground in oceanographic research.

FRIDTJOF NANSEN

The name of Nansen’s specially built ship, (TCO, means “forward” in Norwegian, reflecting both Nansen’s positive philosophy and the state-of-the- art nature of the ship. It was fully electrified, with arc-lamps and a windmill to power the generator when its powerful 220hp engine was not running.

The reinforced hull was built with a rounded profile, so that sideways pressure from the ice would push the boat up rather than crushing it.

REACHING FOR EXTREMES • TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH

FRITDJOF NANSEN

A distinguished figure in the history of polar exploration, Nansen’s scientific career also encompassed the development of early neuroscience techniques. His leadership, organizational skills, and passionate belief in democracy led to a second career as a diplomat before and after World War I. Nansen’s work on famine relief and refugee resettlement was widely honored, and, in 1922, he received the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his achievements.

Nansen was a polymath, as fascinated in meteorology and mathematics as he was in zoology. On his ﬁrst journey to the North in 1882 on board the 8KMKPI, he acquired the habit of making copious sketches of everything he observed. He drew this polar bear in 1927.

ROALD

AMUNDSEN

PIONEERING POLAR EXPLORER AND MAN OF FIRSTS

NORWAY

1872–1928 Practical, pragmatic, and ruthlessly ambitious, Roald Amundsen was one of the great polar explorers of the 20th century. Infatuated with exploring the Arctic, he is best remembered— ironically—for beating Scott to the South Pole in

1911. Meticulous planning, strong leadership skills,

and extensive knowledge of Inuit wilderness techniques equipped him for success whatever the challenge, whether navigating treacherous waters by sea, crossing ice-caps by husky sled, or gliding over the roof of the world by airship.

surviving thick fog and an onboard fire before anchoring at a natural harbor on King William Island for the winter.

They set up a base, which they named “Gjøahavn” (Gjøa’s port) after their faithful ship, building a magnetic variation observatory that would enable the scientific study that was the trip’s official objective. While conducting their research, Amundsen and the crew also learned from the Inuit of the area, mastering such valuable skills as building snow huts, driving teams of sled dogs, and making garments from furs.

After nearly two years of successful scientific study, including calculating the exact location of the magnetic North Pole, the Gjøa raised anchor in August 1905. Amundsen took a westward course through previously unknown channels—some of which were so shallow that the boat had just over 1 in (3 cm) of water beneath its keel—using the ship’s gas engine for maneuverability. Three weeks later, a whaling As a child, Amundsen dreamed of being a polar explorer, his imagination fired by the exploits of fellow-Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen (see pp. 296–99), who almost reached the North Pole in 1895.

Although a career in medicine was chosen for him by his parents, he read accounts of polar exploration in secret and trained his physique to prepare for the rigors ahead. Abandoning medical school after the death of his mother, he joined a sealing expedition to the Arctic in 1894 to gain seamanship skills, then served as first mate on the Belgica during a failed Antarctic expedition of 1897–99. He soon proved his worth, taking command of the vessel after the leader, Adrien de Gerlache, became ill.

THE NORTHWEST PASSAGE

On returning from the Antarctic, Amundsen’s sights turned northward. He soon drew up plans to navigate the Northwest Passage, learning from the mistakes of the ill-fated Franklin expedition (see pp. 292–93) by traveling light and living off the land. In June 1903, he set out from Christiania (now Oslo) in Norway aboard the Gjøa, a small vessel capable of navigating the shallow waters of the Arctic straits, with a crew of just six men. After crossing the Atlantic, the crew made it through the “foul waters” of the Boothia Peninsula,

SOUTH POLE STORY

Amundsen wrote of his South Pole success in The South Pole: An Account of the Norwegian Antarctic Expedition in the Fram, 1910–12, published in 1912.

It was an instant best-seller.

HARDY WAYFARERS

Amundsen and the crew of the Gjøa reached Nome, Alaska, in 1906, after three years of exploring the Northwest Passage. The men had encountered temperatures as low as –63°F (–53°C) and “snow in this severe cold, like sand,” but picked up invaluable knowledge from the Inuit and witnessed such extraordinary sights as the Aurora Borealis, or Northern Lights.

IN HIS FOOTSTEPS

1903–06—Northwest Passage Amundsen and six crew navigate the Northwest Passage for the first time 1910–12—South Pole After a last-minute change of destination, Amundsen leads four companions to reach the South Pole for the first time 1918–25—North Pole aboard the Maud Returning to his first love, Amundsen attempts to drift over the North Pole aboard a ship stuck in the Arctic ice. The Maud drifts back and forth for seven years, during which time Amundsen considers flying instead 1926—North Pole aboard the Norge Amundsen and 15 crew fly over the North Pole on the airship Norge ship from San Francisco was sighted—the Gjøa had passed into navigated waters, meaning that the Northwest Passage had been crossed.

However, in early September the ship became ice-bound once again, and the crew was forced to overwinter at King Point, close to Herschel Island, some 60 miles (100 km) from the Alaska border.

Undeterred, Amundsen made an 800-mile (1,300-km) journey by dog-sled inland to the nearest telegraph station at Fort Egbert in Eagle City, Alaska.

The news broke early to the world’s press on December 5, 1905, when the content of his telegram was intercepted. Returning to the Gjøa, Amundsen completed the final stage of the journey to San Francisco in October 1906.

PLANS UP-ENDED

Back in Norway, Amundsen—now enjoying considerable financial backing thanks to his success—set his sights upon the geographic North Pole. He planned to use the Fram, the specially designed polar-exploration vessel built for Nansen in 1893, to drift over the Pole while frozen into the winter pack-ice. Everything was in place when, in 1909, news arrived that first Frederick Cook and then Robert Peary (see pp. 308–09)— both of whose claims would be contested—had gotten there first. Ever the pragmatist, Amundsen swiftly turned to the South Pole, but kept his plans secret for fear of losing funding. He was also mindful that Robert Scott (see pp. 312–15)

had announced an expedition, so wished to gain the upper hand over his British rival.

Amundsen only made public his actual destination while en route to Antarctica in August 1910. From the island of Madeira he sent letters to Nansen and the Norwegian king, Haakan VII, and telegrammed Scott with the simple message “beg to inform you fram proceeding antarctic.” Given his desire for “firsts,” there can be little doubt that Amundsen deliberately sought an advantage, and Scott would have been well aware of the implications for his expedition. Before they proceeded, Amundsen gave his crew the chance to go home, but none did.

Amundsen serves as a ﬁrst mate on the failed Antarctic expedition of the Belgica 1894–1903 1903–06 1906–10 1910–12 The Fram crossed the Antarctic Circle in January 1911 and dropped anchor at the Bay of Whales in the Ross Sea. The ship then sailed for Buenos Aires, leaving a nine-man wintering party to set up depots at intervals toward the Pole. Amundsen’s closest depot to the Pole was at 82°S, 170 miles (275 km) closer than Scott’s closest, which was at 79°29’S.

RECORDING THE CONQUEST

Reaching the South Pole on December 14, 1911, Amundsen took readings with a sextant and artiﬁcial horizon as evidence. Notes were also left in a tent in case the party failed to reach the Fram.

ROALD AMUNDSEN

By September 1911, Amundsen judged his men sufficiently fit, and on October 19, five men and four light sleds, each pulled by 13 dogs, set out across the crevasse-ridden Ross Ice Shelf.

They reached the Queen Maud Mountains, the biggest obstacle between them and the Pole, on November 11 and spent four hard days crossing them. After reaching the polar plateau via the Axel Heiberg Glacier, onward progress was relatively straightforward. On December 8, they passed the farthest point south reached by Shackleton (see pp. 318–19), then pressed Amundsen’s plane is lost in foggy conditions over the Barents Sea; the wreckage is never found Amundsen and his team sail north to Hobart, Tasmania, where his success is announced on March 17, 1912

INUIT KNOW-HOW

The knowledge gained from the Inuit during the 1903–06 exploration of the Northwest Passage helped to shape Amundsen into a hardened, resourceful polar explorer.

Skills such as making clothing from furs and skins were vital to the success of future trips, but just as critical was careful planning. Amundsen wrote: “Victory awaits him who has everything in order—luck, people call it.” 1912–25 1926–28 E Amundsen retired from exploration in 1926, having fulfilled all his ambitions. British accusations of dishonor over the secrecy of his Antarctic plans in 1910 were said to have hurt him, but no one would question the honor of the manner of his death. In 1928, at almost 60 years of age, Amundsen joined a rescue flight in the search for his friend, Italian airshipman Umberto Nobile, with whom he had flown over the North Pole on his final expedition.

Nobile’s airship had come down near Spitsbergen, and Amundsen’s plane is also thought to have crashed in the fog over the Barents Sea. The wreckage was never recovered, despite recent searches using unmanned submarines.

CHARLES HALL

UNLIKELY LEADER OF AMERICA’S FIRST POLAR PARTY

UNITED STATES

1821–71 A publisher by trade, Charles Hall was driven to the Arctic by a conviction that survivors from Franklin’s “lost” expedition of 1845 were still to be found. As publisher of the Cincinnati Occasional and The Daily Press, he was well aware of the sensation Franklin’s disappearance had caused.

The knowledge of Arctic survival techniques that Hall acquired on his two expeditions in search of Franklin led not only to US-government backing for an attempt on the North Pole, but also proved essential to future polar explorers.

exploration, he managed to raise funds for a search expedition of his own. He set out in May 1860 aboard the whaler George Henry, which was captained by Sidney Budington, a veteran of the Arctic. Also on board was Kudlago, an Inuit with whom Hall had struck up a friendly rapport. On sighting his first iceberg, Hall noted: “all my conceptions of its grandeur were more than realized.” He later landed on an iceberg and reached its summit “using a boat-hook as a sort of alpenstock to aid me.” Hall was born in Vermont in 1821 and received little formal education. He was a blacksmith’s apprentice as a boy, but possessed an inquiring mind that would take him far in life. Fascinated by the searches for the “lost” expedition of John Franklin (see pp. 292–93), Hall spent nine years studying the findings of Francis McClintock, a British Royal Navy officer who had led several searches for Franklin between 1849 and

1859. Hall concluded that there could still be

survivors. Despite having no experience of polar

KING WILLIAM ISLAND

Hall dies at Thank God Harbor in November 1871 Hall planned to hire Inuit helpers and to navigate his way northwest to King William Island, where traces of Franklin’s party had been found. However, the ice proved too thick for travel beyond Baffin Island, so Hall remained there a while to study Inuit culture. He took to wearing a tuktoo (caribou-skin) jacket and pants, and slept head-to-toe with nine others as a guest of his guide, Keyezhune. He especially enjoyed Inuit feasts, eating warm seal’s liver and entrails and endearing himself to his hosts by asking for a second helping.

In the summer of 1862, Hall—guided by English-speaking Inuit couple Ebierbing and Tookoolito—explored the nearby islands.

Spotting pieces of brick among the possessions of an Inuit woman, Hall realized that here were artifacts from English explorer Martin Frobisher’s expedition of 1557–58. “There in my hand was undoubtedly a relic of that expedition which had visited the place only eighty-six years after the discovery of America by Columbus.”

MISSION ACCOMPLISHED

After returning without evidence of Franklin in 1863, Hall failed to raise sufficient funds for a full-scale expedition, partly because the Civil War had broken out. In 1864, he sailed north aboard the whaler Monticello, again piloted by Captain Budington, and accompanied by Ebierbing and Tookoolito.

The trip was to last five years. He traveled north through Hudson Bay, overwintering at Fort Hope on Repulse Bay, just the northwest coast of Greenland to overwinter.

Although his friend Budington was captain of the ship, Hall struggled to assert his command over the large team, and the expedition soon split into factions. Confident that the position of the ship had ideally placed them for a spring attempt on the Pole, Hall made an initial sledding sortie northward. On his return to the Polaris on October 24, he reported stomach cramps. His condition rapidly deteriorated, and he died on November 8, 1871. The expedition suffered a similarly dire fate: the factions separated in the winter of 1872 when the Polaris became trapped in ice, and the two groups were fortunate to be rescued in the spring of 1873.

Hall had complained of feeling unwell after drinking oversweetened coffee, and in 1968 a further clue was found to his macabre end. His exhumed body was shown to contain high doses of arsenic in the hair and nails. Had onboard rivalry spilled over into treachery, or did Hall unwittingly self-administer the poison, a common ingredient in medicines at the time?

Hall’s death bears enough mystery to match that of the object of his fascination—John Franklin.

LIFE IN THE EXTREMES

An image from Hall’s Arctic Researches Among the Esquimaux (1865) shows an Inuit village near Frobisher Bay.

Hall was fascinated by their customs and survival techniques.

ADOPTING INUIT WAYS

Hall was one of the ﬁrst American explorers to adopt Inuit ways and tools, such as these wooden snow goggles.

inside the Arctic Circle.

By 1869, he had traveled the remaining 300 miles (500 km) to the coast of King William Island. There he located the graves of several of Franklin’s men, recovering human remains and several artifacts. Having proven beyond doubt that none of Franklin’s expedition had survived, Hall spent the remainder of the trip living with the Inuit. He was one of the first Americans to show that by following Inuit ways, it was possible to survive in harsh polar regions.

SHARING FRANKLIN’S FATE Hall returned to the Arctic in 1871 with a very different mission. His nine years of experience in the polar field had brought official recognition, and soon after his return to the US in 1869, he was commissioned to lead the first government- funded expedition. With an ultimate goal of reaching the North Pole, $50,000 was spent equipping and preparing his ship, the Polaris.

The expedition left New York in late June 1871, sailing via Baffin Bay into Smith Sound, the strait separating Canada from Greenland.

By August 29, Hall had set a new northerly record for shipping in the Arctic Circle, reaching a latitude of 82°11’N. Turned back by thick ice soon after, the ship put into a bay on

3&"$)*/('03&953&.&4tTO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH ROBERT E. PEARY

CONTROVERSIAL ARCTIC EXPLORER

UNITED STATES

1856–1920 A century after Robert E. Peary claimed to have reached the North Pole, controversy still rages over the veracity of his story. Some have even accused him of fraud, arguing that he could not have made his dash for the Pole in the time he said it took him. Others have set out to prove that his claims were entirely reasonable. Whatever the truth, Peary remains an important figure in polar exploration for his earlier pioneering work in the Arctic, mapping the northern shores of Greenland and Ellesmere Island.

Bob Bartlett blazing a trail, using a pioneering method known as the “Peary System,” in which one man skied ahead of the main party to warn of hazardous pressure ridges and open-water channels. The agility and rapidity of the front man allowed him to set a course for the main party with as few detours as possible. The party also comprised support explorers, whose job was to lay depots along the way for the return journey and to carry essential equipment. In this way, the men earmarked for the final assault kept fresh by carrying a lighter load. One by one, the support parties turned back, leaving six men to make the dash to the North Pole.

PERFECT POLAR CONDITIONS

In the early hours of April 2, 1909, along with his trusted fellow explorer Matthew Henson (see pp. 310–11), and his best Inuit dog drivers, Ootah, Ooqueah, Seegloo, and Egingwah, Peary set off under clear skies for the final leg of the journey. After five long marches in perfect conditions, he took readings and was satisfied that they had reached the ultimate north. He wrote in his journal: “The Pole at last!!! ... my dream and ambition for 23 years. Mine at last.” The six men hurried back from the Pole with such ease that Ootah remarked to Henson: “The devil is asleep or having trouble with his wife, A commander in the US Navy, Peary made the first of several expeditions to Greenland and the Canadian Arctic in 1886. In the course of these first explorations, he lost eight of his toes to frostbite. In 1906, he claimed to have reached a latitude of 87°06’N, a new record for the farthest north yet reached. This was doubted later, since it meant he must have traveled at least 80 miles (130 km)

without making camp. The speed at which Peary claimed to travel was to come under even greater scrutiny three years later.

THE PEARY SYSTEM

On February 27, 1909, Peary led an expedition party of 24 men and 133 dogs from Cape Columbia, located 413 miles (665 km) from the Pole. A MIXED WELCOME HOME

Peary returned to the US in 1909 to a mixed reception. While some were sceptical of his claims, the people of Bangor, Maine, awarded him with the Loving Cup in a public ceremony.

or we should never have come back so easily.” But Peary’s troubles were just beginning as he returned to face a world that did not believe he had reached the Pole. Not only that, but he discovered that it was widely accepted that his former colleague turned archrival, fellow American Frederick Cook, had beaten him to the prize a year earlier. It is now thought that Cook, in fact, fabricated his evidence and did not reach the Pole, but experts remain divided over Peary’s claim.

RETRACING PEARY’S STEPS In 2005, British explorer Tom Avery set out from Cape Columbia to recreate Peary’s dash to the Pole. Avery’s intention was to test Peary’s claim that the journey could be made in 37 days. Using replica sleds and similar equipment—including a steering contraption called an amituk (Inuit for “thingamajig”), Avery beat Peary to the Pole with five hours to spare.

However, the exploration establishment was not convinced by Avery’s achievement, claiming that ice conditions were different. Nonetheless,

Avery stood up to the barrage of criticism by stating that he had proved that it was possible for a man to walk the distance Peary had claimed in the time he had claimed. In the process, Avery had himself set a new record for the fastest surface journey to the North Pole.

Others, however, remain unconvinced. The great British polar veteran Sir Wally Herbert— who definitely did reach the North Pole on foot on April 6, 1969—had put an end to widespread sympathy for Peary’s claim, which had been supported by the National Geographic Society.

Herbert’s book, The Noose of Laurels (1989), offers compelling evidence that Peary had neither the technical expertise nor the time available to carry out the dash to the Pole as he had claimed. If Herbert is right, then the first person to have arrived at the Pole was Alexandr Kuznetsov—by plane on April 23, 1948—and Herbert himself was the first to reach the Pole by a surface route.

Experts from the Scott Polar Research Institute, at the University of Cambridge in the UK, think Peary may have failed to reach his goal by as much as 100 miles (160 km). They do not doubt that Peary himself believed he had made it, but the controversy over his claims remains.

In a career that lasted more than 50 years, Herbert traveled a total of 23,000 miles (40,000 km) through the wastelands of the polar regions.

His greatest feat came in 1968–69, when he led the British Trans-Arctic Expedition. They completed a 3,800-mile (6,100-km) surface crossing of the Arctic Ocean from Alaska to Spitsbergen, passing over the North Pole on the way. The journey convinced Herbert that Robert Peary could not have reached the North Pole.

MATTHEW

HENSON

AFRICAN-AMERICAN EXPLORER OF THE ARCTIC

UNITED STATES

1866–1955 Matthew Henson was an African-American Arctic explorer from Charles County, Maryland.

Orphaned at the age of 11, he made his way to Baltimore, where he was hired as a cabin boy, spending six years traveling across the Pacific, the Atlantic, the South China Sea, and the Baltic.

Henson’s resourcefulness, coupled with his practical skills and ability to learn the ways and language of the Inuit, won him a key role in Robert Peary’s explorations of the Arctic and his attempts to reach the geographical North Pole.

By 1891, with the necessary funds secured, the North Greenland expedition became headline news, and Peary was besieged by applicants. But it was a small team of just six explorers that set out from New York aboard the Kite in June 1891, surviving a battering voyage through pack-ice before arriving at McCormick Bay on the northwest coast of Greenland in late July.

EXPLORING THE INTERIOR

The objective of the expedition was to explore Greenland’s ice cap and gather information to help with planning future attempts on the Pole, but Henson’s first task was of a more practical nature. He was responsible—almost single- handedly—for the construction of Red Cliff House, the wooden hut that would serve as the expedition headquarters. It was during this task that Henson first worked alongside the Inuit, who welcomed him as one of their own. Their help and advice enabled him to master the Inuit language and to gain sledding skills that would be critical to his future success.

Henson gained invaluable practical skills during his six years sailing the oceans, including navigation, carpentry, and mechanical know-how. But it was a chance encounter with Robert Peary (see pp. 308–09) in a fur store in Washington, D.C., that eventually led to his adventures in the Arctic.

Impressed by what he saw, Peary, then a young civil engineer, hired Henson as a valet for a canal- building survey of Nicaragua in

1887. The young man showed great

aptitude in the challenging conditions of the jungle, and his reliability so impressed Peary that he was invited to join an as-yet unfunded expedition to Greenland and the polar ice cap.

FRIEND OF THE NORTH

Carried to the Arctic by a spirit of adventure, Henson took to the ways of the people he found there like no other before him. They were vital to his success.

FIRST-NATION TECHNOLOGY

The Inuit wore snowshoes such as these to walk on deep, powdery snow. Henson used them on Peary’s expedition.

INUIT PROTECTIVE CLOTHING

Henson oversaw the making of clothing from Arctic hare, seal, caribou, and—most prized of all—Polar bear. Garments were made by the Inuit women, who chewed the hides until pliable.

Returning to Greenland in 1893, Henson was frustrated by Peary’s refusal to include him on a sledding expedition. Peary later wrote that Henson was “a hard worker and apt at anything; [he] showed himself, in powers of endurance and ability to withstand cold, the equal of others in the party,” but nevertheless obliged him to carry out menial duties. However, Henson was not one to bear a grudge, so he made the most of the opportunity to spend more time with the Inuit, becoming accepted when he adopted an orphaned boy named Kudlooktoo.

When Peary returned to the camp, determined to overwinter while most of the party returned home, Henson was the only man to support him until another man, Hugh Lee, followed his example.

It was a winter that almost ended in disaster. While traveling in the small whaleboat General Wistar, Peary and Henson were battered by a violent storm—named Anoahtaksoah (“Demon of the Great Ice”) by the Inuit—that nearly drowned them. In 1895, Peary, Henson, and Lee undertook a long

MATTHEW HENSON

than 250 miles (400 km) in 11 marches. Peary asserted that Henson “is a better dog driver and can handle a sled better than any man living, except some of the best Eskimo hunters.”

TO THE POLE

Henson accompanied Peary on several attempts on the Pole itself, reaching 174 miles (280 km) from their goal—the nearest yet—in 1906. Their eighth and final chance came in 1909, by which time Henson was 42 and Peary 10 years his senior. By now, Henson was fluent in the language of the Inuit and had become the vital link-man between Peary and the Inuit helpers. He was responsible for selecting sled-drivers and their dogs and hand-built more than 20 sleds of Peary’s own design. He also tutored less-experienced members of the party, patiently explaining how best to stand to avoid heat loss and how to build an igloo. Henson set out on March 1 with Peary and a team of five, each of whom was in command of their own sled and two others—piloted by Inuit drivers—in order to carry enough supplies to reach the Pole. Their five companions dropped back one-by-one after caching supplies for the Pole party.

Henson, Peary, and four Inuit drivers reached a point that they thought to be the North Pole on April 6, 1909. Henson later wrote, “As I stood there at the top of the world and thought of the hundreds of men who had lost their lives in the effort to reach it, I felt profoundly grateful that I had the honor of representing my race in the historic achievement.” Completely exhausted, Peary was unable to lead the return journey, and it was Henson’s determination that led to their successful return to Cape Columbia on April 23, 1909, having covered more than 500 miles (800 km) in 16 arduous days.

TREACHEROUS TERRAIN

The windswept ice of Ellesmere Island in Canada—base camp on the 1909 expedition—was a dangerous landscape, at times the sea-ice became buckled and uneven, while leads—areas of open water between the ice—posed a constant threat.

HI-TECH STOVE

The 1909 party used this oil stove built by Henson and designed by Peary. It could melt ice and boil water far quicker than other stoves.

journey across 450 miles (725 km) of the ice cap in northeastern Greenland. They were left alone with three sleds and 37 dogs after their Inuit helpers had abandoned them, fearing the god Kokoyah would kill them all. The three men made it back in June, reporting that “the condition of the country did not allow much exploration.” Having shot and eaten all but one of their dogs to survive, Henson vowed not to return to the Arctic “with the strongest resolution … never again! No more! For Ever!” But Henson did return to the Arctic on several expeditions as Peary’s “assistant.” During an 1898 expedition to explore the ice north of Greenland further, Peary found himself so badly frostbitten—he was to lose all but one of his toes—that Henson, having nursed his companion and strapped him to a sled, led the return journey, covering more Despite being Peary’s right-hand man and preferred choice of companion to reach the Pole, Henson’s achievement on the the expedition went unrecognized. In fact, Henson never met Peary again, although the two did correspond over his autobiography A Negro Explorer at the North Pole. While Peary received awards and a Navy pension, Henson took a job in a Brooklyn garage until he was given a government position as a mail carrier at US Customs and only received official recognition in the later years of his life. In 1950, he was honored in a military ceremony at the Pentagon, and in 1954 received a presidential citation from President Eisenhower.
