ROBERT SCOTT

TRAGIC HERO OF ANTARCTICA

ENGLAND

1868–1912 British naval officer Captain Robert Falcon Scott was “bitten by the pole mania” when he tried, and failed, to reach the South Pole in 1902.

He finally made it 10 years later, only to find that he had been beaten there by Norwegian Roald Amundsen. Unlike Amundsen, who had learned from the Inuit how to use dogs in the Arctic, Scott relied too heavily on poorly selected ponies and man-hauled sleds. Partly as a result, he and his four companions all died in the terrible weather conditions of the return journey from the Pole.

On his return to Britain, Scott found himself proclaimed a hero and fêted by royalty, but his eyes were still firmly fixed on the South Pole.

Within two years, he was planning a return to Antarctica to make another attempt. By 1906, however, Scott and Shackleton had had a falling out, and Shackleton led his own expedition, setting another new record for the farthest south yet traveled, but narrowly missing the Pole. Scott knew that he had to act quickly if he were to win the prize himself.

By 1910, preparations were complete, and he sailed for Antarctica on board the Terra Nova with a crew of 65 men, including six veterans of the Discovery. Scott took with him new motor-sleds, which he had tested in France and Norway. He also took dogs and ponies as part of a complex transportation strategy that would rely ultimately on a great deal of brute manpower.

His distaste for the use of dogs as transportation was to result in a fatal misjudgment.

THE RACE BEGINS

In October 1910, Scott received news that the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen (see pp. 302–05) was also heading for Antarctica.

Amundsen himself had been beaten to the North Pole by Robert Peary (see pp. 308–09).

Unlike Scott, he was only interested in “firsts” and so the race to the South Pole was on.

Scott’s first experience of the Antarctic came when he led the National Antarctic Expedition of 1901–04, which included Ernest Shackleton (see pp. 318–19) as Third Officer. Scott’s ship, the specially built research vessel Discovery, landed at Cape Adare on January 9, 1902. During that first Antarctic summer, he made the continent’s first balloon ascent from the Bay of Whales to observe a possible route to the South Pole.

After sheltering for the winter, two expeditions were undertaken. One party headed west in search of the Magnetic South Pole, while Scott set out on November 2 with Shackleton and physician Edward Wilson and headed for the Geographical South Pole. They turned back after setting a new record for the farthest point south yet reached, but still 500 miles (850 km)

short of the Pole. Scott recorded that they returned to base camp at Hut Point because they were “as near spent as any three persons can be.” It was a harrowing return journey and Shackleton, in particular, suffered extreme exhaustion. After that experience, Scott had no illusions about the unforgiving conditions of the Antarctic.

REACHING FOR EXTREMES • TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH Scott’s party spent their first winter at Cape Evans on Ross Island, the southernmost island reachable by sea. They built a large hut, and as the weather abated, established three depots on the route across the Ross Ice Shelf. The men spent the following season reinforcing the depots with supplies.

THE PUSH FOR THE POLE

By October 24, 1911, everything was ready for an attempt on the Pole. Second-in-command Teddy Evans led a party using motor-sleds, while Scott set out with 10 ponies and eight crew members. The two parties came together on November 21 and proceeded along the Ross Ice Shelf, leaving depots of provisions at strategic points. They reached the Polar Plateau on December 21 and Scott selected four Unlike Amundsen, who had learned the value of dogs in the Arctic, Scott had little faith in huskie-power. He took 34 dogs, 19 ponies, and even state-of-the-art motorized sleds, but relied heavily on manpower to haul loads. Scott considered that “no journey ever made with dogs can approach the height of that fine conception which is realized when a party of men go forth to face hardships, dangers, and difficulties with their own unaided efforts.”

BRUTE MANPOWER

CASTLE OF ICE

In this image, the photographer Herbert Ponting captures the moment a dog sled passes in front of a giant ice-castle on the Ross Ice Shelf.

men to join him on the final leg: Edward Wilson, Henry Bowers, Evans, and Lawrence Oates.

The Polar Plateau is a high, forbidding, bitterly cold expanse of land 10,000 ft (3,000 m) above sea level. The five men made slow but steady progress, passing Shackleton’s previous record south on January 9. As they approached the South Pole itself, Bowers spotted a Norwegian marker flag.

Amundsen had beaten them to the prize. The dispirited party themselves reached the South Pole on January 17, 36 days after the Norwegians. Scott’s diary records his feelings on coming second: “The worst has happened ... All the daydreams must go ... Great God!

This is an awful place.” He noted his trepidation in the face of the 800-mile (1,300-km) return: “I’m afraid the return journey is going to be dreadfully tiring and monotonous.”

THE STRUGGLE BACK

They initially made rapid progress, completing the 300-mile (500-km) journey back across the Polar Plateau by February 7. However, bad weather was closing in as they made the dangerous 100-mile (160-km)

descent of the Beardmore Glacier, and rations were running short. Evans’s health had been deteriorating for a couple of weeks, and he collapsed and died on February 17, following a fall near the foot of the glacier.

“I AM JUST GOING OUTSIDE” The remaining four men reached the Ross Ice Shelf safely, meaning that they had completed the most dangerous part of the journey.

However, high winds and low temperatures hampered their progress. Oates had severe frostbite and gangrene, and the aggravation of an old war wound left him barely able to walk. He realized that there was no hope for the remaining men if he continued, and on March 16, he left the tent with the words, “I am just going outside, and may be some time.” He was never seen again.

By March 19, the remaining three men had reached a point just 11 miles (18 km)

1901–04—Leads National Antarctic Expedition Scott’s first taste of Antarctica is a three-year expedition on which he surveys a route to the South Pole on a balloon flight; he makes a first failed attempt to reach the Pole and sets a new record for the farthest south traveled 1910–12—Returns to Antarctica in the Terra Nova On his second expedition, Scott and four companions reach the Pole, only to discover that they have been beaten to the prize by Amundsen, who had planted the Norwegian flag on the Pole 36 days earlier; the dispirited British team struggle back and die just 11 miles (18 km) short of One Ton Depot and safety On his ﬁrst visit to Antarctica, Scott’s attempt at the Pole fails; Shackleton is part of his team, but the men later part ways Exhausted and penned in by the weather, the three survivors make their last camp just short of safety; they die a few days later Shackleton fails to reach the Pole, but sets a new record for farthest south 1910–12 C The Terra Nova lands on Ross Island, where the party build a hut and make a base camp from which they will supply depots across the Ross Ice Shelf A On the return journey, Evans falls as they descend from the Polar Plateau to the Ross Ice Shelf down the Beardmore Glacier; he dies soon afterward B C B A Oates leaves the tent to sacriﬁce himself when he realizes that he is too ill to continue

Scott and his four companions took this folorn picture of themselves at the South Pole on January 17, 1912. Amundsen’s Norwegian ﬂag is in the background.

Not shown on map One Ton Depot and safety (this was the depot placed farthest toward the Pole). However, exhaustion and the terrible conditions forced them to make a final camp. A blizzard made any further progress impossible, and they took shelter in their tent. As their supplies ran out and the storm continued to rage, it became clear that they were not going to make it. Scott’s diary falls silent between March 23 and his last journal entry, dated March 29, when he wrote: “The end cannot be far … Last entry … For God’s sake, look after our people.” He left a “Message to the Public,” explaining how the men had been defeated by the weather, and ending on a defiant note: “We took risks … and therefore we have no cause for complaint, but bow to the will of Providence, determined still to do our best to the last.” A search party found the tent the following summer, and an ice cairn was erected over the bodies as a mark of respect. Judging from the positions of the three bodies, it seemed that Scott had been the last to die. Despite their ultimate failure, Scott and his men quickly became national heroes for the way they had faced adversity and disappointment, although they have since been criticized for aspects of the expedition’s organization, and particularly for Scott’s refusal to take dogs on the final leg of the journey.

Amundsen was deplored in Britain for his secrecy, but in recognition of his achievement, he was invited to speak to the Royal Geographical Society on November 15, 1912, where he was introduced by the president, Lord Curzon, who noted: “Our guest was attended throughout by good fortune upon which we congratulate him.” The Norwegian himself remarked: “I would gladly forgo any honor or money if thereby I could have saved Scott his terrible death.”

SCOTT’S HUT During the British Antarctic Expedition of 1910–12, Robert Scott set up camp on Ross Island at a site he named Cape Evans. The hut—part living quarters, part laboratory—was built quickly from prefabricated sections, with internal walls made from packing cases. Radiating from a central wardroom table and heating stove, the hut was divided into a shared living area (a cubicle provided Scott with additional privacy) and areas for geological, biological, and meteorological lab work. There was a darkroom where photographs could be developed and an annexe for stables where the ponies were housed. The hut became the expedition’s home for three years.

ERNEST

SHACKLETON

ANGLO-IRISH HERO OF ANTARCTIC EXPLORATION

ENGLAND

1874–1922 A charismatic and driven figure, Ernest Shackleton undertook four expeditions to the Antarctic. His first experience was as a member of Captain Scott’s 1901–04 National Antarctic Expedition, but it is for his third expedition that he is most famous. The expedition very nearly ended in tragedy as his ship, the Endurance, became trapped in ice, but, remarkably, the whole crew returned home safely.

“Wanted. Men for hazardous journey.

Low wages. Bitter Cold. Long hours of complete darkness. Safe return doubtful. Honor and recognition in the event of success.” The Endurance sailed from Plymouth on August 8, 1914, reaching South Georgia on October 26. The Aurora team was charged with laying a series of supply depots and was sailing from Australia. On hearing from whalers that there was extensive ice in the region, Shackleton postponed the Endurance’s departure for a month. On December 5, Endurance finally headed off and soon encountered pack-ice, but the crew was able to negotiate its way south, sighting land on January 10, 1915. As they continued south, a six-day gale caught the ship in an ice-drift.

Despite repeated During Shackleton’s second journey to the Antarctic, on the privately funded 1907–09 Nimrod expedition, he had successfully reached a new “farthest point south”: 88°23’S, some 97 miles (155 km) from the South Pole. On his return to London, he began to plan a third expedition, this time to the Pole itself. Before he could raise the funding, however, the Norwegian Roald Amundsen (see pp. 302–05)

reached the South Pole. So Shackleton devised a new plan: a Trans-Antarctic Expedition that would see a party crossing the continent, a journey of 1,800 miles (2,900 km). Shackleton declared the ship his winter station, renaming it “The Ritz.” By mid-July, temperatures were beginning to rise slowly, but he began to have doubts that the ship would be able to withstand the ice pressure. As he feared, the ice had crushed the hull, and on October 24 the ship began to leak badly. The crew abandoned the ship and made camp on the ice. The Endurance finally sank on November 21.

ESCAPING ELEPHANT ISLAND

Shackleton decided to head for some cached supplies on Paulet Island, 346 miles (554 km)

away, by a combination of marching and drifting on the ice. On April 8, 1916, the ice opened up around them and the following day the crew took to their boats. They were within 60 miles (95 km) of Paulet Island, but the ice in that direction was impassable, so Shackleton decided to head for Elephant Island. Making their way slowly through ice floes, the three boats eventually reached open water and landed on Elephant Island by mid-April. It was decided that a small party would sail in the largest boat, the James Caird—just 22½ ft (6.9 m) long— for South Georgia, 800 miles (1,280 km) away.

Accompanied by five of his men, Shackleton set

BOOK OF JOB

Taken with him on the Endurance, Shackleton’s Bible is missing many pages. He ripped them out to reduce the weight of his possessions when the ship was abandoned.

HUT AT CAPE ROYDS

Shackleton’s base for the 1907–09 Nimrod expedition still stands at Cape Royds, on Ross Island, which lies just off the coast of Antarctica.

out on this journey on April 24, with supplies for just one month. The crew sailed through complete darkness for up to 13 hours a day. On the 16th day, they landed at King Haakon Bay on South Georgia, having run out of water.

Leaving behind three men, McNish, McCarthy, and Vincent, on May 19 Shackleton set out with Crean and Worsley to reach the whaling station at Stormness, 22 miles (35 km)

away. They crossed glaciers and mountains over 3,900 ft (1,200 m) high, attaching screws to their boots to form crampons. After failing to descend a high ridge known as the Trident, the men were forced to jump down an immense crest while attached to a small coil of rope, and narrowly avoided being dashed on the rocks.

They finally reached Stormness Bay after traveling nonstop for 36 hours. Worsley boarded a whaler to rescue McNish, McCarthy, and Vincent. Shackleton made three attempts to rescue the crew from Elephant Island, but was foiled by the ice. The 22 remaining crew members were finally rescued on August 30 with the help of a small Chilean navy tug.

Elation at their miraculous escape was short-lived, however, as the crew returned home to discover the horrors of World War I. They put their survival down to the leadership of the man they called “Boss,” and many of them signed up for Shackleton’s final expedition to Antarctica, on which he died of a heart attack.

THE ENDURANCE

On January 18, 1915, the Endurance, Ernest Shackleton’s ship for his Trans-Antarctic expedition, was trapped by ice in the Weddell Sea, close to Antarctica. By the end of February, the vessel was being squeezed by extreme pressures, locked in an ice floe that was moving southwest. “The Boss,” as the men nicknamed Shackleton, described a sound that “resembles the roar of heavy, distant surf. Standing on the stirring ice one can imagine it is disturbed by the breathing and tossing of a mighty giant below.” By November 21, the men watched from an ice floe as the ship sank. So began the remarkable story of Shackleton’s leadership and survival on the ice.

CONQUERORS OF MOUNT EVEREST

INITIAL FAILURE

In the face of such extreme conditions, many previous attempts to scale the mountain had failed. The British climber George Mallory took part in three unsuccessful expeditions to climb the mountain. When asked why, he famously replied “because it’s there.” Mallory and his partner, Andrew Irvine, died on the mountain in 1924, and it is not known for certain if they reached the summit.

The 1953 expedition also looked at first like it would end in failure. Hillary and Tensing had not been the first choice to try for the summit. Expedition leader John Hunt chose fellow Britons Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans to be the first pair to try on May 26. They ran into difficulties 1,000 ft (300 m) from the top and turned back.

Three days later, however, Hillary and Tenzing made their successful bid for the top.

The Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing was a formidable mountaineer, but Hillary, by his own admission, was no “hot shot rock climber.” What the bee-keeping New Zealander lacked in 11:30 a.m., May 29, 1953: the precise time at which Hillary and Tenzing became the first recorded humans ever to stand on the summit of Mount Everest. The peak, also called Mount Chomolungma, straddles the border between Nepal and Tibet in the Himalayas mountain range. The mountain’s peak is one of the most hostile environments on Earth. It is 29,029 ft (8,848 m) above sea level, and the atmosphere at this altitude contains only one-third of the oxygen found at sea level, and this has a technique, however, he made up for in huge reserves of determination. Hillary maintained that “strong motivation is the most important factor in getting you to the top.” Another factor was the use of bottled oxygen to help combat the effects of extreme altitude, something that Mallory had declared to be “unsportsmanlike.”

OXYGEN SUPPLY

Hillary and Tenzing both carried oxygen tanks on their backs. The air is particularly short of oxygen above 26,000 ft (8,000 m).

TENZING AT THE TOP

Hillary took this iconic shot of Tenzing, but there are no pictures of Hillary at the summit. He had forgotten to show Tenzing how to use the camera before the ascent.

1914–86 Many had tried and failed before Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay finally conquered the world’s highest mountain, Everest, in the Himalayas of Central Asia, in 1953. Their achievement brought them worldwide fame, which did not always sit easily on their shoulders. The mountain has been scaled many times since, but remains a formidable challenge, and more than 200 climbers have lost their lives on its slopes.

THE ROOF OF THE WORLD

Standing on top of the world, Hillary and Tenzing paused briefly to admire the view over Nepal and Tibet, plant their summit flags, and take photographs. The media attention that was heaped on the two climbers upon their descent took both men completely by surprise, but their newfound fame came at a price. Speculation developed as to which man was the first actually to set foot on the top. The expedition team leader made the decision to avoid the issue by saying that the men had arrived at the summit at “almost the same time.” But the spirit of the achievement was blighted by rumors that Tenzing had been virtually dragged to the top by Hillary. Later in life, both men wrote in their memoirs that Hillary reached the rounded snowy dome first, with Tenzing five or six paces behind.

After Everest, Hillary had further successes as an expeditioner, most notably in 1958, when he became the first to reach the South Pole overland

Born into an aristocratic family, Fiennes spent eight years in the army before beginning his remarkable career as an adventurer.

Fiennes was the ﬁrst person to reach both the North and South Poles by a surface route, and the ﬁrst to cross Antarctica on foot. In 2000, he suffered severe frostbite in an unsuccessful attempt to be the ﬁrst to reach the North Pole solo and unsupported. He later amputated several of his necrotic ﬁngers himself using a saw in his garden shed. Despite subsequently undergoing major heart bypass surgery, Fiennes showed no signs of slowing down and, in 2009, aged 65, he became the oldest person ever to climb Everest.

Since the chances of ﬁnding shelter at high altitude are slim, one of the most essential items of equipment for any climbing expedition is a tent. A high- altitude tent must provide shelter from the extremely strong winds and heavy snowfall encountered on high slopes.

Without shelter from the elements a climber risks exposure and death.

Edward Whymper summed up the requirements of a mountaineering tent as being “sufﬁciently portable to be taken over the most difﬁcult ground, while combining lightness with stability.” For Alpine climbing, Whymper used a tent that consisted of four poles, a length of cord, a large sheet of muslin for the roof, and a large piece of plaid rubberized cotton for the ﬂoor and internal walls.

Maurice Herzog and three fellow climbers lost their tent during a nightmare descent from Annapurna, Nepal, in 1950.

MAKING CAMP ON HIGH GROUND

THE TRICKS OF

THIN AIR

WHITE HELL

High altitude can have a debilitating effect on the human body, ranging from fatigue and strokes to cerebral and pulmonary edema—an accumulation of water in the brain or lungs—which can be fatal.

Snow reﬂects 80 percent of UV light compared to just 20 percent for sand, so snow blindness is a risk. The mind can become confused due to low oxygen. High altitude also brings intense cold and the added risk of hypothermia and frostbite.

They eventually found shelter at the bottom of a 15-ft (5-m) crevasse after fellow-summiteer Louis Lachenal had fallen into it. The climbing team found it more comfortable than the prospect of hacking a cave out of the ice, but had only one sleeping bag between four, so placed their feet inside it in the hope of preventing further frostbite. Herzog’s condition worsened until he was unable to walk—he owed his life to a Sherpa named Pandi who carried the 200-lb (90 kg) Frenchman on his back.

Avalanches are an ever-present danger in the high mountains. The 1922 British Everest Expedition was abandoned after seven sherpas were killed by an avalanche, while on a German expedition to Nanga Parbat, in the Himalayas, in 1937, seven climbers and nine sherpas were killed when their camp was buried beneath an avalanche. Most victims, if not killed outright, die through lack of oxygen. The recent invention of the “avalung,” a breathing apparatus worn on the chest, reduces this risk.

HIGH ALTITUDE

When asked why he wanted to climb Everest, British climber George Mallory retorted “Because it’s there!” He was probably exasperated at being asked to justify why climbers risk their lives in what the French mountaineer Lionel Terray called the conquest of the useless. Climbing mountains purely for the sake of it probably began with the 1786 ascent of Mont Blanc by Jacques Balmat and Horace-Bénédict de Saussure. Almost a century later, Edward Whymper scaled the Matterhorn, the last of the great Alpine peaks, after which attention moved to the high mountains of the Himalayas.

TOUGH TRANSPORTATION

HAULING FOOD

Reaching a high summit is often dependent on knowledge of previous climbs. If attempting an unexplored peak, a reconnaissance trip is vital. The successful 1953 Everest expedition utilized photographic data from previous attempts and information from a 1951 reconnaissance expedition.

BEASTS OF BURDEN

The best high-altitude pack animals are those native to the locality. In the Andes, llamas boast padded hooves that give greater traction over mountain terrain. In the Himalayas, yaks can haul loads to 20,000 ft (6,000 m).

Once beyond the range for animals, manpower is essential. None of the Everest expeditions would have succeeded without sherpa porters and climbers.

Edible ﬂora and fauna is scarce at high altitude, so rations were carried by pack animals or porters. Despite this, in 1868 George Hayward was forced to eat his yak after reaching the source of the Yarkand River in the Karakorum Mountains. For the successful ascent of Everest in 1953, food supplies were organized with military precision. Basic “compo” (composite) rations fed 14 men for a day on oatmeal biscuits, sausages, butter, jam, cheese, chocolate, meat, baked beans, and canned fruit. Assault rations contained oats, powdered milk, sugar, jam, cookies, banana bars, cheese, salt, cocoa, tea, and soup. Luxury items included canned fruit, coffee, sardines, and rum.

EDMUND HILLARY

COPING WITH EXTREMES

At high altitude, both the terrain and the weather can be treacherous. Equipment failure or a missed footing can result in a fall of hundreds of yards, which—even if not immediately fatal—can result in death due to the impossibility of hospital treatment. With the ever-present danger of frostbite, the properties of the climbing boots used are of great importance. For the 1953 Everest expedition, boots were specially made with a layer of insulation that protected the foot from exterior moisture and from perspiration. The boots were also ﬁtted with an outer covering of a rubber-coated stockinette. Making the boots tested the capacity of the manufacturers to the full, especially since Edmund Hillary wore size 12 boots, while some of the sherpas wore only size 6. Both the climbers’ outer clothing and the expedition tents were made of a cotton-nylon mix, treated with a waterproof coating. The tents were of the two-man Meade design that had remained unchanged since the 1920s, while larger domed tents were also used for communal sleeping and as mess tents at lower altitudes.

HIGH ALTITUDE

Some of the earliest evidence of undersea exploring comes from about 3200bce, when decorative objects made from mother-of-pearl appeared in Thebes, Greece, in quantities that could not have been sourced from beachcombing alone. Sponges, pearl oysters, red coral, and murex shells—yielding purple dye—were also of high value at the time. The 17th-century English physicist Edmond Halley later explained how these early free divers harvested their quarry: sponge divers were “accustomed to take down in their mouths a piece of sponge soaked in oil, by which they were able to dive for a longer period than without it.”

TALES OF EARLY DIVING

In the 5th century bce, the Greek writer Herodotus wrote of the skill and daring of Scyllias and his daughter Cyane in his Histories.

This pair of divers were employed by the Persian king Xerxes to gather treasure from his sunken galleys. In revenge for a broken promise by Xerxes, the pair dived to sever the anchors of his ships before swimming 9 miles (14 km)

underwater. Human physiognomy makes this an unlikely tale, but some have suggested that the pair’s escape was aided by the use of hollow reeds as breathing tubes. According to a description in the Technica Curiosa by 17th-century German physicist Gaspar Schott, a demonstration took place in 1538 before Emperor Charles V at Toledo by “two Greeks [who] let themselves down under water in a large inverted kettle with a burning light and rose up again without being wet.” Schott also described Lorica aquaticus (“aquatic armor”) illustrated by a man walking into water wearing a small diving bell reaching to his feet.

DIVING BELL

In 1691, Halley patented a revolutionary design for a diving bell. A truncated wooden cone measuring 3 ft (1 m) in diameter at the top and 5 ft (1.5 m) at the base, it contained 60 cubic ft (1,700 liters) of air supplied from barrels weighted with lead.

Leather pipes fed air to a diver outside the bell, while a companion sat on wooden staging within the bell.

During descent, the bell paused at 12 ft (3.5 m) to allow water to be expelled by air from one of the barrels, while a stop-cock at the top of the bell could be adjusted to release stale air.

During experimental dives, Halley sent messages to the surface in the empty air barrels. He remained underwater at a depth of 60 ft (18 m)

for up to 90 minutes. Describing the revolutionary nature of his patent, he wrote, “This I believe to be an invention applicable to various uses, such as fishing for pearls, diving for corals, sponges, and the like in far greater depths than has hitherto been thought possible.” In 1790, engineer John Smeaton further improved the design by introducing a continuous supply of air, which was pumped into the bell from a cable on board ship.

FROM BELL TO HELMET

Although Halley’s bell enabled divers to remain underwater for considerable periods of time, it offered little flexibility to the diver or scope for exploration. German inventor Augustus Siebe was the first to attempt individual diving equipment. In 1819, he designed a metal helmet that was attached to a waterproof canvas jacket, forming an “open” suit that was supplied with air by a hose from the surface. However, the jacket could fill with water if the diver fell or lost his footing—a potentially fatal design flaw. In 1837, Siebe designed a “closed” underwater suit. It weighed

With some modification, this form of underwater dress remained in use for a century or more.

However, although the suit allowed flexible movement of the diver, the cable that supplied air from the ship on the surface restricted how far the diver could travel to the length of the cable itself. In 1860, however, two French inventors, Benoît Rouquayrol and Auguste Denayrouze, patented an invention named the aérophore—a compressed air device attached to the back of the diver. Rouquayrol, a mining engineer, originally created the device for pit-rescue work but with Denayrouze, a French naval officer, adapted the equipment for underwater use. Initially, the aérophore was an uncomfortable system, but by 1865, the two men patented a new version that was worn with Le Groin—a glassed helmet—the precursor of the modern diving mask. Finally, in 1943, Jacques Cousteau (see pp.330–33)

invented his revolutionary aqualung, which led to the complete independence of the modern diver.

WILLIAM BEEBE

DEEP-SEA EXPLORER AND OCEANOGRAPHIC PIONEER

UNITED STATES

1877–1962 Naturalist and undersea explorer William Beebe pioneered the use of technology to study undiscovered deep-sea life-forms in the 1930s.

Already an acclaimed ornithologist, he used the newly invented bathysphere to uncover the world beneath the waves in a series of deep-sea dives off the Bahamas, coming face-to-face with marine specimens that had never been seen before. Beebe’s prolific writing, coupled with his enthusiasm for the natural world, greatly boosted public interest in the marine environment.

Born in Brooklyn, New York, and educated at Columbia University, Beebe’s early career as a naturalist began as Assistant Curator of Birds at the Bronx Zoo. He undertook research expeditions to Singapore, Mexico, the Galápagos Islands, and the jungles of South America, conducting birdlife surveys and collecting specimens for the New York Zoological Society’s collection. STUFF OF ADVENTURE

The bathysphere was an international sensation that appealed to an audience of all ages, such as the youthful readership of this 1937 UK monthly publication.

INTO THE BLUE

On August 15, 1934, the bathysphere was lowered into the waters off Bermuda for its record half-mile dive.

international renown and achieved critical acclaim for A Monograph of the Pheasants, a major illustrated study of pheasants in Asia.

PLUMBING NEW DEPTHS

By the age of 51, Beebe’s interest in oceanography was becoming more than just a passing diversion. Following initial expeditions above the waves aboard the Arcturus, he shared his desire for a way to examine deep-sea subjects at close quarters with his friend, former US President Theodore Roosevelt, an avid naturalist. At the time, the farthest depth for safe diving was just 200 ft (60 m), below which the pressure caused physical problems for the diver. Many of the fragile undersea life- forms would also be crushed or disfigured by the changes in pressure if brought back to the surface. Beebe consulted various engineers and diving specialists before being introduced in 1928 to Otis Barton, a wealthy industrialist who had invented the bathysphere, a submersible craft that he described as a “hollow steel sphere on the end of a cable.” The interior

WILLIAM BEEBE

it was agreed to that more than five seconds’ radio silence would signal to the surface crew that the divers were in trouble. When they reached a depth of 2,000 ft (600 m), the final traces of light from the surface disappeared and they were surrounded by pitch blackness.

Beebe later commented, “It is only a psychological mile-post, but it is a very real one. We had no realization of the outside pressure but the blackness itself seemed to close in on us.” The pair became overnight media sensations, with front-page headlines in the New York Times and an enthralled readership. In 1932, Beebe made a radio broadcast from the bathysphere to an audience of millions across the US.

Their craft was buffeted by swells and both men were injured, before Beebe signed off from the depths: “Otis Barton and I bid you farewell from a depth of 670 meters [2,200ft]

beneath the surface of the Atlantic Ocean, off Bermuda.”

RECORD-BREAKERS

Barton and Beebe’s final expedition together came in 1934 in a National Geographic-sponsored dive. The pair broke the half-mile barrier to

DEEP-SEA MACHINE

Beebe and Barton pose with the bathysphere during the 1934 National Geographic expedition. The circular entrance hatch, which weighed 400 lb (180 kg), was bolted shut after entry to seal the occupants safely inside.

pressure was maintained at sea-level rates, while at a depth of 1,400 ft (425 m) the pressure on the hull would be 1,000 times greater. Strengthened quartz glass was used for two port-holes, while a third held a powerful searchlight. A solid rubber cable carried oxygen, electricity, and a telephone line from the surface-ship down to the chamber.

FIRST DIVES

The first dives in the bathysphere took place off the coast of Bermuda in June 1930.

Attached by cable to a barge, the Ready, Beebe and Barton made several test-dives in the sphere. Beebe wrote of their findings in his best-selling account, Half Mile Down: the light changed to “this indefinable blue … It seemed to me that it must be like the last terrific upflare of a flame before it is quenched.” As the dives went deeper, Beebe noted the bioluminescence of several of the sea creatures, many of whom emitted their own light. During the dives, Beebe kept in constant telephone contact with his assistant, Gloria Hollister.

Such were the potential dangers of the dive, reach a record depth of 3,028 ft (923 m).

However, Beebe’s interest did not lie in simply breaking records. His motivation was to be able to see and record the marine life that lived at these previously unexplored ocean depths.

Beebe’s explorations were among the first to be accessible to the wider public—US audiences were thrilled by the adventurous tales recounted in National Geographic magazine—but the breathless prose of his accounts veiled the serious scientific endeavors of his work.

Lacking modern cameras, Beebe noted the details of his discoveries and later described them to an artist, whose drawings would often become the subject of criticism and debate among fellow scientists.

Beebe was at the forefront of oceanographic study in the 1930s, and the legacy of his unlocking of the secrets of the oceans was a public captivated by the wonders of the deep. He remained active well into his eighties, returning to his first love of ornithology. From the veranda of his home in rural Trinidad, he observed nesting birds through a pair of custom-built giant binoculars mounted on a tripod.

BALL OF STEEL

The bathysphere was a simple sphere 4¾ ft (1.5 m) in diameter, made from cast steel 1 in (2.5 cm) in thickness. Oxygen was supplied from a pressurized cylinder, while fans circulated the air over pans of soda lime to absorb exhaled carbon dioxide.

THE FIRST FLOATING LABORATORY

The modern science of oceanography effectively began with the great voyages of HMS Challenger between 1872–76.

The ship covered nearly 69,000 nautical miles (208,000 miles or 130,000 km) as a team of scientists took samples and measured the depths of the oceans. The expedition was organized by the Royal Society of London and led by Professor Charles Wyville Thomson, who removed the warship’s guns to make room for two fully equipped laboratories. Upon their return, Thomson’s assistant, John Murray, supervised the production of a mammoth 50-volume report on their findings.

CHARISMATIC EXPLORER OF THE DEEP

FRANCE

1910–97 The great oceanographer Jacques-Yves Cousteau was also a filmmaker, author, and inventor. Along with two colleagues, he invented the aqualung, which for the first time enabled divers to swim freely underwater for long periods.

Using this new equipment, Cousteau pioneered the use of color underwater photography and film, revealing to his viewers a new world beneath the waves. He was a committed environmentalist, using his films to highlight the damage human activity was causing to the oceans.

At the time, a single oxygen source was fed via an air line to the diver from his ship, technology that had not changed since the 1870s. Cousteau realized that air would need to be compressed to enable divers to carry a useful amount with them. But although compressed air systems had been developed in the 1920s, none had been able to control the pressure of the air flow— crucial to a diver, as the pressure of the flow needs to change with depth. The outbreak of World War II enabled Cousteau to develop his ideas. While interned at Toulon, Cousteau and colleagues Frédéric Dumas and Émile Gagnan developed a prototype breathing apparatus that would transform human knowledge of the depths.

Cousteau was born in the Gironde region of France before the family moved to New York in 1920, where Cousteau learned to dive. After returning to France in 1930, Cousteau bought his first movie camera, which began a life-long fascination with film. He entered the French naval Academy, hoping to become an aviator in the Naval service. However, during his final months of study, he suffered severe injuries in a car accident, which partially paralyzed his right arm.

CHANGE OF CAREER

Unable to continue with his career as an aviator, Cousteau was posted to the French naval base at Toulon, where, encouraged by Philippe Tailliez, a diving expert and naval officer, he began to explore the underwater world of the Mediterranean Sea from the beaches around the base. With goggles, rubber flippers, and an adapted camera, Cousteau was able for the first time to record the diversity and beauty of sea life. Although

WORLDWIDE SUCCESS

Cousteau’s account of his early adventures underwater, The Silent World (1953), became an international best-seller, selling more than five million copies. He followed the book with a documentary of the same name, taking his crew of 25 on a voyage of discovery through the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. He captured some of the earliest color footage of coral reefs, rare fish, and the attack behavior of sharks. By the time The Silent World won an Academy Award for best documentary in 1957, the pattern of Cousteau’s life was firmly established. He became the director of the Oceanographic Museum of Monaco, and experimented further with the technology, including the descent of a specially adapted pressure-proof camera to a depth of 4 miles (7 km), where new species of starfish were found.

UNDERWATER LIVING

In 1962, off the coast of Sudan, Cousteau built the first of his experimental “Conshelf” underwater living capsules. Divers could stay The new “aqualung” developed by Cousteau and his colleagues was revolutionary—it provided a canister of compressed air that was kept at the same pressure as the external water depth. On Cousteau’s first dive using the prototype, he reached a depth of 59 ft (18 m). He described the sensation: “I experimented with all possible maneuvers, loops, somersaults … delivered from gravity and buoyancy, I flew about in space.” The new equipment was taken up by the US Navy, which called it the SCUBA (self-contained underwater breathing apparatus) system.

At the end of the war, Cousteau was able to convince his superiors that there was an immediate practical use for the aqualung in clearing German mines from the Mediterranean and other ports around the French coast. In 1946, he founded the French Naval Undersea Research Group. He remained in the navy for another 10 years, developing other underwater equipment, including a camera that could be used at a depth of up to 2,000 ft (600 m).

INTO THE SILENT WORLD

From 1950, Cousteau carried out larger scale underwater exploration, diving from a series of ships all called Calypso. The first, a refitted minesweeper, acted as a scientific base, capable of carrying a complement of 28 people, and became the backdrop to Cousteau’s films.

In addition to the innovation of a viewing gallery at the prow of the ship and the inclusion of eight submarine port holes, Cousteau was ever mindful of the needs of the diver. The Calypso included “a wet diving well down through the hull, entered through the galley, so that divers could go into the water amidships, the most stable point on the hull. In bad weather they could avoid passing through the waves at the sides. From cold dives they would climb into the warm kitchen.” In 1951, the Calypso set sail from Toulon for Cousteau’s first expedition to the Red Sea, where he and his divers would study coral reefs. He described the sea as “… a corridor of marvels— the happiest hours of my diving experience have been spent there … The reef of Shab Suleim was an intaglio structure with porches of coral, winding couloirs, and countless narrow cracks aswarm with beings waiting in the wings like walk-on players at the opera.” Cousteau in his customary poetic language described how “The

Unlike previous underwater breathing apparatus, the aqualung is an open-circuit system, meaning that exhaled air does not go back to the tank.

This is why divers must always breathe in through their mouths and out through their noses. The revolutionary part of the design, however, is the diving regulator. This makes sure that the pressure of the air in the tank is lowered to a breathable level, and also adjusts to compensate for the increased pressures of lower depths.

ENVIRONMENTALIST

In 1968, Cousteau combined all his expertise to present a series of color television documentaries. The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau introduced his viewers to marine biology and gave them a better understanding of the undersea world.

The programs presented a romantic view of sea life, but at the same time addressed many issues relating to the protection of this delicate environment. In 1977, a new series, Cousteau Odyssey, concentrated on marine conservation issues.

He saw his programs as the best way to promote wider concern for the environment, saying that “one protects what one likes.” As an underwater pioneer, Cousteau left a remarkable legacy, anticipating many of the environmental concerns we have today.

DIVING SAUCER

Cousteau invented the two-person diving saucer with engineer Jean Mollard in 1959. It is a submarine that can explore at depths of up to 1,300 ft (400 m).

3&"$)*/('03&953&.&4tEXPLORING THE DEEP The Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico is pitted with strange sinkholes in the ground known as cenotes. These plunge through the water table into vast networks of caves that are only now being mapped and explored. Of these, the Ox Bel Ha system is the longest underwater cave in the world. As of May 2009, 110 miles (180 km) of passages have been explored, with much yet to discover. New technology, such as GPS, driver propulsion vehicles (DPS’s), and rebreathers (a special breathing set that provides oxygen mixed with recycled, exhaled gas), enables divers to explore deeper into the cave systems every year.

The waters of the caves are exceptionally clear as a result of rainwater ﬁltering through porous limestone, revealing a world of life-forms previously unknown to science. Some are ancestors of marine animals that became trapped in the caves and evolved over time to survive in fresh water and complete darkness. The pathways of the caves have many junctions, pits, and turnings, and navigating them is very dangerous.

HUMANS

UNDERWATER

SUNKEN TREASURE

All mammals display reﬂex reactions to submersion in water. The average human heart will slow to a rate 10–25 percent below its normal surface rhythm, enabling the body to redirect oxygen from the bloodstream to vital organs.

On deep dives, blood circulation to the extremities reduces and then stops completely, a condition known as peripheral vasoconstriction.

With the invention of modern scuba- diving equipment in the 1940s (see p. 332), divers could for the ﬁrst time explore shipwrecks, ruined cities, crashed aircraft, and other submerged sites.

Marine archeologists have salvaged gold from 16th-century Spanish galleons returning from the New World, cannon, ancient amphoras of wine, and even corpses, using airbags to raise artifacts to the surface. Most famously, the wreck of the Titanic, which sank in 1912, was located in the Atlantic Ocean by ALVIN, a manned ocean submersible, in 1986.

UNDER THE WATER

Today, the world may seem fully charted and connected, with few wildernesses left untrodden or unsurveyed by satellite. Yet there remains one frontier that technology has only recently opened to exploration: the ocean depths and underground waterways of the Earth. Modern scuba-diving equipment, submersibles, and ROVs (remotely operated vehicles) are revealing a previously hidden world of undisturbed wrecks, labyrinthine cave systems, and life-forms so strange they have made scientists rethink their ideas about the nature of life on Earth and elsewhere in the solar system.

FIRST SUIT

In 1797, German Karl Klingert invented the ﬁrst diving suit, made from waterproof leather.

CAVES OF WONDER

Here, divers ascend through a cenote in the Yucatán Peninsula.

The caves beneath the cenotes are yielding many biological discoveries, including compounds that have anticancer properties.

UNDER THE WATER

THE ALIEN OCEAN FLOOR

In 1977, scientists from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in California made a discovery that would overturn one of the most fundamental beliefs about the nature of life on Earth. Sending the submersible ALVIN 6,900 ft (2,100 m) to the East Paciﬁc Ocean ﬂoor, they discovered bizarre, chimneylike structures, belching out superheated water and minerals from the planet’s crust.

Surrounding these hydrothermal vents were large communities of fauna, including giant tube worms and scaly-footed gastropods, which subsist by converting the heat and minerals from the vents into food—a process known as chemosynthesis. In other words, life was thriving in places where sunlight—thought until then to be the source of all food, energy, and, therefore, life—had never penetrated. Huge ﬁelds of vents have since been found.

THE SEA, ONCE IT CASTS ITS SPELL, HOLDS ONE IN ITS NET

OF WONDER FOREVER

JACQUES COUSTEAU

DANGERS OF THE DEEP

Scuba-diving has revolutionized underwater exploration by giving divers the freedom of having their own air supply. The activity is extremely dangerous, however.

Each year the sea claims the lives of divers who have run out of air, been struck by a vessel, become tangled or trapped, or even attacked by a dangerous animal.

International safety codes apply to all categories of diver. Scuba divers follow strict predive routines to ensure maximum safety. On a boat dive, predeparture tide times and up-to-date weather reports for the dive area are essential. Scuba equipment is checked for malfunction, and the air-gas mix and average air consumption are calculated in advance, with a reserve to allow for an emergency. In cold water, the protection level of exposure suits is also assessed to ensure that the dive time is possible without risk to the diver.

DIVE BUDDIES

The buddy system is vital to scuba-diving safety. Divers operate in pairs of “buddies” and are expected to monitor each other during a dive and ensure that the other does not get into trouble. Buddies stay close to each other throughout the dive so that they can help in an emergency, if necessary, sharing their air supply until they can return to the surface. Buddies use a system of internationally recognized hand signals to “speak” underwater. Some divers may make solo dives without a buddy, particularly when they want to focus on activities such as underwater photography rather than their buddy’s welfare. Only divers with hundreds of hours of experience are allowed to dive solo.

BEYOND THE BOIL

The vents can reach temperatures of 752°F (400°C), but do not boil due to the pressures at such a depth. The vents are clustered around unstable areas of the Earth’s crust.

The first people known to have studied the solar system were the ancient Babylonian, Egyptian, and Assyrian astronomers. Their observations were preserved from distant antiquity by later Greek scholars. In 150bce, Hipparchus—and later, Ptolemy in his Almagest—used the evidence of Egyptian astronomers to interpret celestial events, proposing that the Earth was a stationary, fixed plane at the heart of a heavenly vault, on which the Sun, Moon, and stars were “fixed” in a series of outer spheres.

ASTRONOMICAL ADVANCES

It was not until the revolutionary work of Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus in the 16th century that our understanding of the Earth’s position in relation to the Moon and stars was radically transformed. Copernicus made the crucial realization that the Sun was at the center of the solar system, which later influenced the work of German mathematician Johannes Kepler and Italian scholar Galileo Galilei. Kepler’s rules of planetary motion, formulated in 1605, would inform the theory of universal gravitation proposed by the English physicist Isaac Newton. This in turn was later used for the calculation of how much rocket power was needed to break free of planet Earth’s gravitational pull.

ROCKET POWER

From the 13th century, rockets began to be developed for use in warfare. A crude form of short-range weapon capable of causing alarm and surprise was developed in medieval China. By the late 18th century, the English inventor William Congreve had refined military rockets, demonstrating his first solid-fuel-powered model in 1805. Metal-cased and with much greater targeting accuracy, his invention laid the foundation for the development of the modern rocket.

SCIENCE FICTION

In the 19th century, writers such as Jules Verne and H. G. Wells wrote stories of space travel that inspired the future scientists of 20th-century travel. Verne described a fantastical journey to the Moon in De la Terre a La Lune (“From the Earth to the Moon,” 1865) while Wells described an invasion from Mars in The War of the Worlds (1898). The feats of their space-traveling heroes were impossible with the technology of the time. Without a continuous source of oxygen to enable combustion, a rocket could not operate in the vacuum of outer space.

In 1903, the Russian writer Konstantin Tsiolkovsky proposed that rockets could be propelled into space in his avant-garde work The Investigation of Space with Reactive Devices, which combined mathematical theory with ambitious futuristic plans for space stations, satellites, and interstellar transportation.

TURNING FICTION INTO FACT

The invention of a rocket-fueled propulsion system in the early 20th century by US scientist Robert H. Goddard allowed the first guided- rocket research to take place. Inspired by Wells’s writings as a boy, Goddard registered 214 patents for a host of inventions relating to rockets while working for the US Department of War at Clark University from 1914. By 1920, his reports described the potential for an unmanned rocket to reach the Moon and signal its arrival by detonating a flare device.

Ridiculed in the press, Goddard moved to New Mexico to continue his research, building models and conducting test flights with support from the Smithsonian Institution. He soon proved his critics wrong, successfully launching the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926. Reports of Goddard’s work spread throughout the scientific

RACE FOR THE MOON

After the war, the first exploratory space probes were launched in the Russian Luna and US Pioneer programs of the 1950s. YURI GAGARIN

THE FIRST MAN IN SPACE

SOVIET UNION

1934–68 From a humble childhood on a Soviet collective farm, Yuri Gagarin rose to become the most famous person in the world in 1961.

Through a combination of determination and good luck (he was just the right size for the space capsule), Gagarin was chosen for the first-ever manned space flight, spending a little under two hours in orbit in the spacecraft Vostok 1. On his return, he became an international star and the embodiment of Soviet technological prowess in the burgeoning space race with the United States.

had given meaning to his life. Having become a skilled pilot of light aircraft, he soon decided he wanted to fly professionally. In 1955, Gagarin was accepted into the Soviet military training program for MiG fighter pilots at Orenburg on the Ural River.

THE SPACE RACE BEGINS

The year Gagarin began his training as a fighter pilot, Russian scientist Leo Sedov called a press conference in Copenhagen, Denmark, to announce the USSR’s plan to put a satellite into space. The announcement sparked the start of the “space race” between the United States and the Soviet Union, as both powers began to invest heavily in research with the goal of beating the other into space. One of the leading figures in the world of Soviet space engineering was Sergei Korolev. He was chief designer at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, located east of the Aral Sea. In 1954, Korolev had developed the R-7 Semyorka rocket, which was capable of launching satellites. On October 4, 1957, Sputnik 1, the first unmanned space craft, was launched.

Yuri Gagarin was born in the village of Klushino in western Russia. His education was interrupted by the outbreak of World War II, after which the Gagarin family moved to Gziatsk, a town nearer to Moscow. At the age of 21, Gagarin left to study at an industrial college at Saratov on the Volga River, and learned to fly with the city’s flying club in his spare time. As a teenager, he had witnessed the crash landing of a Soviet fighter plane close to his family home, and the image of the pilots emerging from the aircraft had left a deep impression on him. He described the thrill of his first flight as one that PILOT OR PASSENGER?

The engineers of Vostok 1 were unsure whether Gagarin would be capable of operating the craft in the weightlessness of space. As a result, all the ﬂight controls were operated from the ground and Gagarin was in effect a passive passenger. In case of emergency, provision was made for Gagarin to unlock the manual controls using a code placed in an envelope by his side.

EMERGENCY RATIONS

In case the engines failed, Gagarin had 10 days’ worth of food to see him through until the craft came down.

Vostok 1’s orbit ended when its braking engines were turned on.

YURI GAGARIN, TO STARTLED LOCALS WHEN HE LANDED

YURI GAGARIN

3&"$)*/('03&953&.&4tINTO THE SOLAR SYSTEM The Russians continued to develop their rocket test flight program, sending animals to heights of some 280 miles (450 km) to establish the physiological impacts of weightlessness, along with additional testing on the effects of cosmic radiation. The scientific evidence confirmed that it would be possible for the human body to withstand the conditions.

TRAINING FOR SPACE

In 1959, a special commission selected 200 pilots from the Russian Air Force for pretraining. Gagarin was selected alongside 19 other prospective cosmonauts for advanced training. They were put through rigorous weightlessness training, simulated conditions for eating and drinking, writing, and operating the radio from a mock-up cabin of the Vostok craft. The training staff included the Russian polar explorer Nikolai Kamanin, who would go on to become the Head of Training for all future cosmonauts.

Kamanin was responsible for selecting the location for Star City near Moscow. This secret Soviet urban facility opened in June

1960. It was a completely self-contained

settlement that served not only the scientific and technological requirements of the space program, but also included schools, stores, and medical facilities for the families of the cosmonauts and scientists. The settlement was strictly off-limits to ordinary Soviet citizens. By April 5, 1961, the original 20 candidates for the flight had been whittled down to two: Gagarin and Gherman Titov. Just four days before the launch date, Kamanin finally decided on Gagarin with Titov as backup.

In final training, it was Gagarin who had met the strictest psychological and physiological criteria for the first man in space travel. In addition, weighing 154 lb (70 kg) and standing just 5 ft 2 in (157 cm) tall, he fit the payload profile required for the flight. Gagarin was not in control of the spacecraft: the Vostok was to be remotely controlled by radio from Baikonur since no one was sure what effect weightlessness would have on Gagarin’s mind and body during the flight. The space craft was designed so that Gagarin sat with his back to the reentry nose-cone of the space craft, in a cramped compartment with a diameter of just 7½ ft (2.3 m), in front of which was positioned the parachute for the craft’s reentry.

Based on the official Soviet accounts, on April 12, 1961, Gagarin calmly walked to the launch pad shortly after breakfast, and with a few delays during countdown, Vostok 1 successfully launched, to Gagarin’s shout of “Poyekhali!” (“Let’s Go!”)

LAUNCHED INTO HISTORY

Vostok 1 blasted off at 9:07 a.m. Moscow time. Its rockets burned for longer than expected, resulting in an orbit at a height of 203 miles (327 km) rather than the intended 143 miles (230 km).

INTO SPACE

This first space journey took just 108 minutes to complete its circumnavigation of the globe after entering orbit. The Soviet coverage of the orbit, released after his successful return, repeated Gagarin’s brief radio reports during the flight. While passing over South America, for example, he stated simply: “Flight proceeding normally, am feeling fine.” Gagarin attained a speed relative to the Earth’s surface of 17,400 mph (28,000 kph) at a height of some 203 miles (327 km) above sea level. According to the Russian journal Medical Worker, Gagarin ate a combination of liquid and paste-form food during the flight, both of which had been his favorites during simulations. As rumors of the Russian achievement spread around the world, the Soviet News Agency, TASS, released a rather dry announcement in confirmation: “History’s first flight in outer space, accomplished by the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin in the space ship Vostok, has made it possible to draw the immensely important scientific conclusion that manned flights in space are practicable.”

A SECRET LANDING

The manner of Gagarin’s return to Earth was not revealed by TASS. It is now known that he exited the capsule at a predetermined point of reentry, and made a parachute drop from a height of 23,000 ft (7,000 m) to the landing site, near the Volga River, 15 miles (24 km) south of Saratov. For 30 years after his flight, this fact was kept a closely guarded state secret, and official accounts stated that Gagarin had returned to Earth in his spacecraft. It was believed that this would mark his flight as an even more significant achievement in the Soviet Union’s ongoing rivalry with the United States.

According to reports, rather than waiting

YURI GAGARIN

to be found by the helicopter that had been despatched to collect him, Gagarin walked away from his parachute to be greeted by the landing team, before passing on his best wishes to the Russian people.

Gagarin’s achievements were to be grandly celebrated in Moscow, where President Nikita Krushchev showered the cosmonaut with the highest honors (Gagarin would become a deputy of the Supreme Soviet and Commander of the Cosmonauts). Krushchev described Gagarin fondly as a “space swallow,” after the crew’s nickname for Vostok 1: the Swallow.

COLD WAR VICTORY

Aside from the scientific and technological success of the orbit, in the context of the Cold War, the Soviet achievement was a catalyst for the American space program.

The world responded to the Soviet Union’s successful orbit with a mixture of admiration, disbelief, and, in the case of the United States, dismay. Some commentators in the United States complained that “everyone remembers Lindbergh—but who remembers the second man to fly the Atlantic?” Meanwhile, Gagarin became an international celebrity, and made a series of public appearances around the world. He returned to Star City eager to make a second space flight in the new Soyuz series space craft, and was initially disappointed to be given a secondary role to his colleague Vladimir Komarov. Disappointment turned to devastation when his friend died on reentry as the capsule plummeted to Earth after its parachute lines became entangled Gagarin went on to take the role of deputy training director for cosmonauts at Star City, but continued to crave the thrills of his flight career. At the age of 34, he returned to

ROCKETMAN

Following his death, statues of Gagarin were erected all over the Soviet Union. This one, with the cosmonaut standing in the shape of a rocket, is in Moscow.

flying, piloting the latest generation MiG jets.

He died on March 27, 1968, when his plane crashed during a training flight from the Chkalovsky Air Base near Moscow. The cause of the crash has never been established. At the time of his death, Gagarin had begun training for a second space mission.

LANDING MODULE

Parachutes were attached to the landing module to slow its descent. However, it had always been intended that Gagarin would eject several miles above the surface.

The Soviet scientists did not know whether living organisms would survive space flight, so it was decided that a test flight should be carried out using a dog. Laika was launched into space on November 3, 1957. No provision was made to return her to Earth, and she died a few hours after the launch. She had proved, however, that it was possible to survive in weightless conditions.

SPACE DOG

MARKING THE SUCCESS

Gagarin’s ﬂight was commemorated on this Soviet postage stamp. The achievement was portrayed by the Soviet authorities as an example of the success of their political system.

Korolev was the head Soviet rocket designer in the 1950s and ‘60s, and is considered by many to be the Father of Astronautics.

A trained aircraft designer, Korolev fell victim to Stalin’s purges in 1938 and spent six years in prison. On his release, he was put to work designing rockets, and was a key ﬁgure in the development of intercontinental missiles that could carry nuclear warheads over long distances. In the 1950s, his attention turned to space as he was appointed head of the Soviet Space Program. Korolev oversaw the successful Vostok and Sputnik programs as the Soviet Union surged ahead of the United States in the space race. He was working on a plan to put a man on the Moon when he died suddenly in 1966.

FIRST HUMAN TO SET FOOT ON THE MOON

UNITED STATES

b. 1930 Aeronautical engineer, aviator, and astronaut Neil Armstrong holds a unique place in the history of space exploration and, indeed, the history of humankind. A talented test-pilot who clocked up flights in more than 200 aircraft, Armstrong was selected as one of the first astronauts in the US government’s space program. As commander of the Apollo XI lunar landing mission—an appointment made partly because of his lack of ego—he had the honor of being the first human to set foot on the Moon.

In 1947, Armstrong began a degree in aeronautical engineering at the US Naval Aviation College. Two years later, he saw active service, flying as a fighter pilot in the Korean War (1950–53), before completing his degree in

1955. He went to work as

a test pilot at the Lewis Flight Propulsion Laboratories in Cleveland, Ohio, and at NASA’s Flight Research Center in Dryden, California.

By 1962, his skills as an engineer, administrator, and pilot made him a natural fit for the new astronaut training program at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). His first space flight took place in 1966 as commander of the Gemini VIII mission, with fellow-astronaut David Scott as pilot. The mission achieved the first docking of craft in space when the Gemini joined with an unmanned Agena rocket, but came close to disaster when an electrical malfunction In the mid-1940s, the ultimate dream of most American teenagers was a driver’s license and a car. Not so for Armstrong, whose interest in aviation grew from making model aircraft and reading plane and flight magazines, to financing his own flying lessons with a series of part-time jobs. He learned to fly in a two-seater Aeronca 7AC Champion at an airport near his home in Wapakoneta, Ohio, and earned his private pilot’s license by the age of 16—although he still couldn’t drive a car.

LUNAR LANDING

On July 16, 1969, the crew of NASA’s Apollo XI mission—Neil Armstrong, Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin, and Michael Collins—began their epic space flight, blasting off from the Kennedy Space Center. Four days later, Collins remained in the command module Columbia as Armstrong and Aldrin embarked in the Eagle, the fragile lunar-landing craft, and touched down in the Sea of Tranquility at 3:17 p.m.

Eastern Standard Time (EST) on July 20. Armstrong reported: “Houston, Tranquility Base here, the Eagle has landed.” The relief at Mission Control was palpable: “We copy you on the ground ... We’re breathing again.” The world’s largest

CUSTOMIZED DESIGN

The Apollo XI insignia, depicting an eagle bearing an olive branch, was designed by astronaut Michael Collins.

SUPERSONIC SPACECRAFT

The Saturn V rocket propelled the command vessel Columbia, which was attached to the rocket’s tip, through space at 25,000 mph (40,000 kph).

WALKING ON THE MOON

The footprints left on the Moon by the ﬁrst astronauts will remain undisturbed for time immemorial because there is no atmosphere and so no wind to blow the imprints away.

NEIL ARMSTRONG

television audience yet watched as Armstrong commenced EVA (extra-vehicular activity), taking his first tentative step onto the surface of the Moon before uttering the immortal words: “That’s one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.”

MAGNIFICENT DESOLATION

Aldrin joined Armstrong 19 minutes later, exclaiming: “Beautiful, beautiful … magnificent desolation …” With their body weight just a sixth of that on Earth, the two explored the lunar surface, staying within 300 ft (100 m) of the Eagle. After leaving a US flag and a Soviet medal in honor of Yuri Gagarin (see pp. 338–41), they set up a range of experiments, took photographs, and gathered 47 lb (21 kg) of Moon-rock and soil samples before returning to the landing craft.

The mission was not without mishap—while maneuvering inside the cramped Eagle, a plastic circuit controlling the rockets that would lift the craft into orbit was broken. Calm and resourceful, the men pushed a plastic pen into the vacant slot to act as a switch. It served its purpose—the Eagle launched and safely rejoined the Columbia.

Armstrong spent just two hours and 48 minutes walking on the Moon, but the achievements of Apollo XI marked the opening of a new chapter in humankind’s ambition to explore the stars. For Armstrong though, once was enough—he did not fly another space mission, joking on his return to Earth: “No matter where you travel, it’s nice to get home.”

PLAQUE OF PEACE

A plaque bearing the signatures of all three Apollo XI astronauts and President Nixon was left as a memorial on the Moon’s surface.

COMMAND

MODULE

The command and service modules are commonly described as the “Apollo spacecraft” and were used, along with the lunar lander, during NASA’s Apollo space program from 1967 onward. The command module is a cone-shaped structure containing a pressurized compartment housing the crew, equipment bays, and systems controls. A docking tunnel linked the command module to the lunar lander. Behind the command module, the service module held the fuel, water, and the main engine.

POST-APOLLO

EXPLORATION

THE NEW FRONTIERS

Just eight years after the first manned space flight of Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, the United States successfully landed a man on the Moon as part of its Apollo program. Optimism over the possibilities for future exploration proved unfounded, however, as the enormous cost of space programs became prohibitive.

took part in the experiments and research.

By the end of its third mission in 1974, Skylab had orbited 3,900 times, passing over 75 percent of the Earth’s surface. It used solar panels to generate its electricity, affording the astronauts such comforts as solid foods and a collapsible shower enclosure.

THE SPACE SHUTTLE

NASA embarked on the next stage in the development of its manned space program in 1981, with the launch of the first space Following the success of Apollo 11, public interest in the remainder of the Apollo missions diminished. The annual cost of the program was some $3 billion, and such high levels of spending had become politically unjustifiable for the US government. Apollo 17 returned to Earth on December 19, 1972, and humans have not been back to the Moon since.

SCIENCE IN SPACE

From the early 1970s, the focus of the US space missions switched to the development of a reusable orbital program. Skylab, the first experimental space station, orbited at a height of 270 miles (430 km) above the Earth’s surface and proved that humans could live and work in space. Skylab’s first three-man crew took off on May 14, 1973, for a 28-day mission at zero gravity. Over three missions, scientists carried out the first detailed study of the Earth from an orbiting spacecraft. The operation was truly international, and scientists from 28 nations shuttle, Columbia, from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The shuttle was a reusable craft, capable of docking with the International Space Station. Its flight controls were completely computerized, using “fly-by-wire” technology originally developed for fighter pilots, which reduces the risk of mechanical error. The part

MARS EXPLORER

The ﬁrst NASA Mars Rover was successfully landed on Mars in 1997. As of 2010, two Rovers are sending back images and analyzing samples from the surface of the planet.

of the shuttle that returns to Earth, the Orbiter, carries between five and seven crew, and its payload can accommodate large satellites, such as the Hubble Space Telescope, which was carried into orbit in April 1990 (see right). To date, there have been 114 missions, with the loss of two shuttles. The Challenger exploded in January 1986, 73 seconds after liftoff, while the Columbia was destroyed during reentry to the Earth’s atmosphere on February 1,

2003. In both cases, the entire crews

were lost. NASA plans to retire the three remaining space shuttles in 2010.

Eventually, they will be replaced by the new generation Orion craft.

SPACE STATION

Construction of the International Space Station (ISS) began in 1998, and is scheduled for completion in 2011.

The completed station will comprise 16 pressurized modules, which have been sent into orbit and docked with the previously docked sections of the station. The ISS is a collaborative project between Russia, the United States, Japan, and Europe, and as of 2010, is the largest artificial satellite ever to be sent into space. It has been continuously staffed since November 2000 and is expected to remain operational until

2020. One of the ISS’s main scientific goals is

the assessment of systems that could be used on future manned flights to the Moon or Mars.

After a 40-year hiatus, the project to transport human beings to other parts of the solar system could soon be taken up again in earnest.

POST-APOLLO EXPLORATION

The Hubble Space Telescope has been sending back images of deep space from its orbit around the Earth since 1993. Away from the distorting effects of the Earth’s atmosphere, it has given us views of galaxies so distant that their light is billions of years old. It is scheduled to be replaced in 2014 by the infrared James Webb Space Telescope.

SHUTTLE SERVICE

The ﬁrst space shuttle, Columbia, took off from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 12, 1981, 20 years to the day after Yuri Gagarin made the ﬁrst manned space ﬂight in Vostok 1.

The shuttle completed 37 orbits in a successful 55-hour mission before returning safely to Earth, making an unpowered landing at the Edwards Air Force Base in California.

FUTURE SCIENCE

EXPLORATION

DISCOVERING THE FUTURE OF HUMANKIND

Much of today’s scientific research and exploration centers on the need to understand human impact on the Earth. Multidisciplinary teams comprising geographers, geologists, microbiologists, and others, work on international projects using the latest in high-technology equipment, often remotely from space, to observe and model changes in the world around us.

The algae help to absorb carbon dioxide from the Earth’s atmosphere. These discoveries enable us to understand the impact of the dust in a future, drier world, as well as revealing precisely how the climate has changed in the recent past—vital information that allows the modeling of future climate change.

BENEATH THE OCEANS

Scientists from the United States Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) are expanding our knowledge of the deepest places on Earth. The scientists use high-tech equipment such as the robotic submersible Nereus to monitor the movement of the Earth’s tectonic plates, and

WINDS OF CHANGE

Officially the dustiest place on Earth, the Bodélé Desert Depression in Northern Chad is an unforgiving landscape. Howling winds whip up millions of tons of white dust, which in turn are blown as far away as the Amazon Rainforest. But the region was not always so inhospitable. Six thousand years ago, North Africa was wetter, and the area contained one of the largest freshwater lakes in the world— about the same size as the Caspian Sea—filled by rainfall draining from Central Africa and what is now the central Saharan Desert.

Scientific research has shown that the lake extended as far as Nigeria and Niger. It is now a chalky-white lake bed, and the dust is made not of sand, but nutrient-rich diatomite, the remains of microscopic organisms that once lived in the lake. International teams of scientists have established the age of the fossil lakes and have discovered how the dust brings added fertility to the soils in the Amazon region and contributes nutrients to the Atlantic Ocean, which in turn help to increase algal growth.

a remote monitoring unit called REMUS, which uses sonar techniques to map areas of the seabed in lanes of overlapping widths—a technique that is known as “mowing the lawn.” Data is enhanced using high-resolution cameras built into the submersibles, providing new insights into the composition of the Earth’s crust and mantle at ocean floor level. This assists scientists who predict natural disasters such as volcanoes, earthquakes, and tsunamis. The WHOI also records, maps, and finds samples of hitherto unknown seafloor communities of flora and fauna, which in turn inform research into the possibilities of life elsewhere in the solar system.

GLACIAL WATERS

The glaciers that drain the Greenland Ice Sheet, calving fleets of icebergs into the Arctic Ocean, are now thinning and retreating at a dramatic rate. Scientists are exploring the effects of distinct phenomena affecting the vulnerability of melting ice sheets to warming.

Every single quart of glacial melt water contains up to one million microbial cells, which are released each spring and summer when the ice thaws. Teams from Russia, Norway, and the UK have collaborated to study

DEEP DIVER

In May 2009, Nereus made the deepest dive ever achieved, reaching a depth of 6.8 miles (10,902 m) to the Mariana Trench on the Paciﬁc Ocean ﬂoor, the deepest point on Earth.

WORK IN PROGRESS

DESERT DUST

During ﬁeld research in the Bodélé Depression, scientists endure choking dust and viciously high temperatures.

glaciers at varying stages of melt. In addition, the research has revealed that glaciers are thriving ecosystems and that the microbes that colonize them may actually be accelerating their melting.

DNA tests have enabled scientists to see how cryoconite (which comprises microorganisms, dead organic matter, and mineral debris) forms and influences the ice environment, and how its presence can increase the absorption of solar radiation by up to 30 percent. Glaciologists are now trying to understand how this will affect the future movement of ice sheets, and how increased melt water will impact on salinity levels in the Arctic Ocean.

POLAR ADVANCES

Rapid developments are also taking place in the field of polar science. The study of subglacial lakes first began in the late 1960s with Russian radar data from Lake Sovetskaya in the Eastern Antarctic. From the 17 known subglacial lakes in the 1970s, satellite imagery has shown that the number today stands at 145 and is increasing, indicating that the polar ice sheets are melting at an alarming rate. Analysis of these interconnected lakes is showing their dynamic role in the system of ice flow and balance in Antarctica.

In addition to the study of the way climate affects the poles, scientists are also using innovative techniques to explore more fundamental scientific questions. By drilling holes in the Antarctic ice sheet, which have a high degree of transparency, it has been possible to capture neutrinos, a form of subatomic particle, which, when captured, shed light on the nature of stars, black holes, and dark matter in the universe.

FUTURE SCIENCE EXPLORATION

One of the most ambitious scientific projects ever conceived is taking place more than 300 ft (100 m)

under the ground at CERN, a research center in Switzerland. The Large Hadron Collider is a circular tunnel 17 miles (27 km) long, through which tiny protons are accelerated to nearly the speed of light and crashed into each other. By analyzing the fallout from these high-speed collisions, scientists are hoping to explore some fundamental questions about the universe, such as why objects have mass and what dark matter may be. If we can discover what happened when the universe was born, we will have a better understanding of its future.

THE ADVENTURE SCIENCE

ICE CAVE

Scientists may spend weeks at a time under a layer of ice over half a mile thick, living in and studying ice caves that form under glaciers. The scientists monitor the microbial life thriving in glaciers and the rate at which the ice is melting.

The Smithsonian Institution—the world’s largest museum and research complex—includes 19 museums and galleries and the National Zoological Park.

The total number of artifacts, works of art and specimens in the Smithsonian’s collections is estimated at 137 million.

The bulk of this material—more than 126 million specimens and artifacts—is part of the National Museum of Natural History.

In addition, the Smithsonian maintains

1.5 million library volumes, including rare

books and 89,000 cubic feet of archival material. Among its vast holdings are many documents, portraits, and artifacts related to explorers and their journeys, from the Lewis and Clark expedition, to Stanley and Livingstone, to the Apollo moon missions.
